title: North Carolina Water and Sewer Lines Contractor - Online Exam Prep Course
description: North Carolina Water and Sewer Lines Contractor - Online Exam Prep Course Prepare for the North Carolina Water Lines and Sewer Lines Contractor examination with a structured online course built around the trade knowledge, safety requirements, installation practices, and contractor responsibilities covered by the exam. This course includes 6 months of course access, giving you time to study at a steady pace, revisit difficult subjects, and practice working with the reference materials connected to the North Carolina classification. Water and sewer line contracting requires knowledge across several technical and regulatory areas. Candidates must understand ductile iron pipe installation, concrete pipe installation, trench and excavation safety, grading, bedding, joining, backfilling, compaction, erosion control, utility-location procedures, liens, contractor law, and North Carolina licensing responsibilities. The course organizes these subjects into a practical preparation structure that helps you move through the exam outline without treating every topic as an isolated lesson. The North Carolina Water and Sewer Lines Contractor Online Exam Prep Course is designed for candidates preparing to serve as the qualifier for a contractor license, experienced utility professionals reviewing for the examination, and applicants who need a focused way to organize a large reference list. The course supports trade-focused review while helping you understand which books address the major examination subjects. Because this is an open-book examination, preparation involves more than memorizing definitions and installation steps. You must recognize the subject of a question, select the correct reference, locate the applicable section, and interpret the information within the testing time. Reference navigation, technical understanding, and repeated practice work together to create a stronger exam-preparation strategy. The listed books are used to support course study and examination preparation. Unless a separate package specifically states that books are included, the reference books are purchased separately from the online course. What You Get Online Course Access: 6 months of course access. Trade-Focused Review: Organized study covering safety, ductile iron pipe, concrete pipe, excavation, grading, erosion control, business, law, and contractor responsibilities. Reference Navigation Guidance: Preparation focused on understanding which reference applies to each major examination subject. Practice-Oriented Preparation: Study structure designed to reinforce terminology, installation concepts, regulatory knowledge, and question-solving skills. Flexible Study Format: Review the course during the six-month access period according to your work schedule and exam timeline. Exam Details The North Carolina Water Lines and Sewer Lines examination is associated with the PU (Water Lines and Sewer Lines) contractor classification. Examination eligibility is determined by the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors, and PSI administers the examination after the candidate receives approval. Examination: North Carolina PU (Water Lines and Sewer Lines) Testing provider: PSI Number of questions: 45 Time allowed: 120 minutes Required passing score: 70% Exam format: Computer-administered, open-book examination The official content outline assigns six questions to safety and three questions to general knowledge. Underground utility concrete pipe installation accounts for 10 questions, while underground utility ductile pipe installation accounts for another 10 questions. Excavating and grading accounts for nine questions. The remaining examination subjects include liens, erosion and sedimentation control, One-Call requirements, and laws and regulations. These categories contain fewer questions, but they remain important because every correct response contributes to the required passing score. Concrete pipe and ductile iron pipe installation together represent a substantial portion of the examination. Candidates should understand material handling, trench preparation, foundations, bedding, placement, joining, fittings, alignment, support, backfill, compaction, testing, and inspection. Safety and excavation knowledge should be studied alongside the installation subjects because field conditions affect every stage of underground utility work. Open Book Test The North Carolina Water Lines and Sewer Lines Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing their own approved references to the testing center. The examination provider does not supply a personal reference set. Open-book testing rewards familiarity and organization. With 45 questions and 120 minutes, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes and forty seconds per question. That time must cover reading the question, recognizing the subject, selecting the correct publication, locating the information, and choosing an answer. The course supports a reference-based preparation method. Safety questions should direct your attention toward the construction safety standards. Ductile iron pipe questions should lead to the installation guide. Concrete pipe questions should lead to the concrete pipe and box culvert reference. Questions involving excavation notification, sedimentation control, contractor law, liens, and licensing require preparation with the corresponding study materials. Current PSI instructions permit approved references to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the exam. Permanent tabs may be used, but removable flags are not permitted. Notes may not be written on tabs, and references may not contain handwritten notes, loose papers, or unauthorized attachments. The current PSI bulletin identifies the 2007 edition of Concrete Pipe & Box Culvert Installation as the listed exam-room reference. The course reference list includes Concrete Pipe and Box Culvert Installation, 2019 for study. Candidates taking a specified edition into the testing center must follow the edition listed in their current PSI examination bulletin. Licensing Steps Review the classification. Confirm that PU (Water Lines and Sewer Lines) corresponds with the work the applicant or business plans to perform. Complete the license application. Submit the required application to the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. Meet the applicant requirements. Applicants must satisfy the Board’s age, character, financial responsibility, application, and background-review requirements. Identify the qualifier. The applicant must designate the individual who will satisfy the examination requirement for the classification. Select the license limitation. Choose the limitation that matches the size of projects the business intends to undertake. Receive examination eligibility. Once the application is approved for testing, the candidate receives an eligibility letter and scheduling instructions. Register with PSI. Use the information issued through the eligibility process to schedule the examination. Prepare for the examination. Use the online course, content outline, and applicable references to review every tested subject. Take the examination. Bring the required identification and only the references and materials permitted under the current testing rules. Complete the licensing process. Follow the Board’s instructions concerning examination results and remaining application requirements. Passing the examination is one part of the licensing process. It does not automatically issue a North Carolina contractor license. The Board must approve the applicant and confirm that all applicable licensing requirements have been completed. State Requirements The North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors regulates the PU (Water Lines and Sewer Lines) classification. The classification covers construction work on water and sewer mains, water service lines, and house and building sewer lines as defined by the North Carolina State Building Code. The scope also includes water storage tanks, lift stations, pumping stations, and appurtenances connected with those facilities. Pavement patching, backfill, and erosion-control work performed as part of qualifying water and sewer construction are included within the classification. Applicants must identify a qualifier who has satisfied the applicable examination requirement. The contractor license belongs to the approved individual or legal entity, while the qualifier provides the examination qualification connected to the classification. North Carolina contractor licenses are issued with limitations that affect the value of projects the licensee may undertake. Applicants must meet the financial responsibility requirements associated with the requested limitation and provide the business and organizational information required by the Board. Underground utility contractors must also understand excavation notification, trench safety, erosion and sedimentation control, site restoration, utility conflicts, and coordination with other trades. The examination reflects both technical construction knowledge and the responsibilities of operating as a contractor. Reference Books The course supports preparation with the following examination and study references: North Carolina Occupational Safety and Health Standards for the Construction Industry, with Latest Available AmendmentsCovers construction safety requirements relevant to underground utility work, including trenching, excavation, protective systems, inspections, access, spoil placement, hazardous atmospheres, equipment hazards, and worker protection. Installation Guide for Ductile Iron PipeAddresses receiving, handling, storing, laying, joining, cutting, tapping, restraining, testing, and backfilling ductile iron pipe. It also supports review of fittings, gaskets, joint assembly, deflection, alignment, and polyethylene encasement. Concrete Pipe and Box Culvert Installation, 2019Supports study of concrete pipe and box culvert handling, foundations, bedding, placement, line and grade, joint assembly, haunch support, backfill, compaction, inspection, and installation quality. North Carolina Excavation Safety Guidelines, 2022 or LaterExplains excavation-notification responsibilities, utility-locate requests, proposed excavation markings, tolerance zones, damaged facilities, safe-digging practices, and coordination with underground facility operators. North Carolina Administrative Code, Title 15A, Chapter 4 Sedimentation Control, Including the Latest AmendmentsAddresses administrative requirements for land-disturbing activities, erosion-control plans, runoff management, stabilization, inspections, enforcement, and sedimentation-control responsibilities. North Carolina General Statutes Chapter 113A, Article 4 Sedimentation Pollution Control Act of 1973Provides the statutory framework for sedimentation-pollution control, including regulatory authority, required plans, prohibited conduct, enforcement, and responsibilities associated with land-disturbing construction. Contractor’s Guide to Business, Law and Project Management - North Carolina General Contractors Edition, 10th EditionCovers contractor business organization, contracts, estimating, project management, financial management, risk, insurance, employment practices, safety administration, liens, and North Carolina contractor responsibilities. Pipe and Excavation ContractingProvides practical study material involving underground pipe construction, trenching, excavation, equipment, estimating, productivity, dewatering, bedding, pipe placement, backfill, compaction, and project planning. Laws and Regulations Applicable to General Contracting in the State of North CarolinaSupports study of contractor licensing statutes and rules, classifications, limitations, qualifiers, applications, prohibited conduct, regulatory authority, and contractor obligations. The reference books are not identified as included with the online course. They may be purchased separately or obtained through an applicable book package. Exam Room Approved Books The current PSI bulletin identifies the following references for use in the North Carolina Water Lines and Sewer Lines examination room: North Carolina Occupational Safety and Health Standards for the Construction Industry, with Latest Available Amendments DIPRA Installation Guide for Ductile Iron Pipe, 2007, Revised 2012 Concrete Pipe & Box Culvert Installation, 2007 Edition The excavation guidelines, sedimentation-control materials, contractor business guide, pipe-contracting book, and North Carolina laws and regulations publication are study references that are not allowed in the examination room. Candidates should prepare with the edition required by their current examination bulletin and inspect all permitted references before the testing appointment. Exam-room books must comply with PSI rules concerning binding, highlighting, permanent tabs, notes, and added materials. Test Information and Study Materials Begin your study plan with ductile iron pipe and concrete pipe installation. Together, these subjects account for 20 of the 45 examination questions. Review how each material is handled, installed, joined, supported, tested, and protected. Learn the differences between rigid and flexible pipe installation concepts and how trench conditions affect system performance. For ductile iron pipe, focus on unloading, storage, trench preparation, pipe laying, cleaning, lubrication, gasket placement, push-on joints, mechanical joints, fittings, cutting, tapping, restraint, allowable deflection, testing, polyethylene encasement, and backfill. For concrete pipe, review foundations, bedding, line and grade, lifting, placement, joint preparation, haunch support, backfill zones, compaction, inspection, and repair considerations. Understand how bedding and surrounding soil support contribute to the performance of an installed concrete pipe system. Safety preparation should cover trench protective systems, inspections, access and egress, spoil placement, water accumulation, hazardous atmospheres, suspended loads, mobile equipment, underground installations, and personal protective equipment. Study the conditions that require protective action rather than memorizing safety terms without context. Excavating and grading is another major examination category. Review trench preparation, soil removal, dewatering, equipment selection, bedding elevation, line and grade, utility conflicts, backfill placement, compaction, surface restoration, and safe access to the work area. Use the additional references to study One-Call requirements, erosion and sedimentation control, liens, licensing, and contractor law. Because these materials are not available in the exam room, the related concepts should be understood before the testing appointment. How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal 1 Exam Prep helps North Carolina Water and Sewer Lines Contractor candidates turn a broad technical and regulatory outline into an organized study plan. The online course supports focused review across pipe installation, safety, excavation, grading, erosion control, business practices, and contractor law. Six months of course access gives you time to build a consistent study routine instead of trying to cover every subject immediately before the test. You can revisit difficult installation concepts, reinforce terminology, review contractor responsibilities, and continue practicing with the references throughout the access period. The course emphasizes reference navigation where applicable. Candidates are encouraged to connect each examination subject with the correct book, become familiar with indexes and chapter structures, and practice locating technical information under timed conditions. Practice-oriented preparation also helps identify weak areas. A candidate who understands ductile iron pipe but struggles with sedimentation control can devote additional review to environmental requirements. A candidate familiar with excavation may need more practice with concrete pipe bedding, joints, or haunch support. 1 Exam Prep provides a realistic study structure without promising a particular examination or licensing result. Consistent review, hands-on industry experience, reference familiarity, and careful exam-day performance all contribute to a candidate’s preparation. Frequently Asked Questions How long do I have access to the course? The North Carolina Water and Sewer Lines Contractor Online Exam Prep Course includes 6 months of course access. Is the examination open book? Yes. The North Carolina Water Lines and Sewer Lines examination is open book, but only references approved under the current PSI rules may be used in the testing center. Are the books included with the online course? The listed books are study and exam references. They are not identified as included with the online course and may be purchased separately. How many questions are on the examination? The examination contains 45 questions. How much time is allowed? Candidates are allowed 120 minutes to complete the examination. What score is required to pass? The required passing score is 70%. What subjects have the most questions? Concrete pipe installation and ductile pipe installation each account for 10 questions. Excavating and grading accounts for nine questions, while safety accounts for six questions. Does the course cover business and licensing subjects? Yes. The preparation structure includes contractor business practices, laws, liens, licensing responsibilities, One-Call requirements, and erosion and sedimentation control. Does completing the course qualify me to take the examination? No. Examination eligibility is determined by the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors through its application process. Does passing the exam automatically issue a contractor license? No. Passing the examination is one part of the process. The Board must approve the applicant and confirm completion of all applicable licensing requirements. Does the course guarantee that I will pass? No. The course provides organized study guidance, trade review, reference-navigation support, and practice-oriented preparation. Examination results depend on the candidate’s knowledge, preparation, experience, and performance.

Masonry construction involves more than placing brick and concrete masonry units. Contractors must understand materials, layout, bonds, mortar, grout, reinforcement, flashing, wall ties, anchors, control joints, expansion joints, lintels, veneers, structural walls, fire-resistant construction, scaffolding, workplace safety, permits, inspections, contracts, business management, and contractor licensing responsibilities. Trade-Focused Review: Study guidance covering masonry materials, brick, concrete block, mortar, grout, reinforcement, wall systems, safety, codes, administration, business, and licensing subjects. Reference Navigation Support: Preparation designed to help candidates identify which book applies to a question and locate information more efficiently. Exam Details The North Carolina Masonry Construction Contractor Exam evaluates knowledge associated with masonry materials, construction methods, workplace safety, building-code requirements, masonry standards, administrative procedures, and contractor responsibilities. Preparation should include concrete masonry units, brick, mortar, grout, reinforcement, anchors, wall ties, flashing, weep systems, lintels, veneers, structural walls, movement joints, specialty masonry, tools, scaffolding, permits, inspections, business practices, laws, regulations, and licensing responsibilities. Some questions may require a direct lookup in an approved reference. Other questions may depend on trade knowledge developed through experience and study. Candidates should understand masonry terminology and common construction practices well enough to recognize which reference applies before beginning a search. Questions involving masonry materials, mortar, grout, reinforcement, structural walls, connections, workmanship, inspection, quality assurance, or technical specifications may require ACI 530/530.1-13. State Requirements The North Carolina Masonry Construction specialty classification applies to qualifying masonry installation performed with or without mortar or adhesives. The classification may include brick, concrete masonry units, gypsum partition tile, pumice block, lightweight masonry products, fire-clay products, refractory construction, rough-cut stone, dressed stone, marble panels, slate units, structural glazed tile or block, glass block, and solar-screen masonry units. Masonry projects may involve structural walls, nonbearing partitions, veneers, foundations, columns, pilasters, fireplaces, chimneys, retaining elements, arches, lintels, reinforcement, mortar, grout, flashing, weep systems, anchors, wall ties, and movement joints. Contractors may also need to comply with engineered plans, building permits, inspections, fire-resistance requirements, manufacturer instructions, quality-assurance procedures, occupational-safety standards, and local approval requirements. Unit type, mortar, grout, reinforcement, wall configuration, flashing, anchors, and structural details may vary by project. title: North Carolina Unlimited Electrical Contractor - Online Exam Prep Course
description: North Carolina PSI Unlimited Electrical Contractor - Online Exam Prep Course Prepare for the North Carolina Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination with an online exam prep course designed around the technical, licensing, business, calculation, and plan-reading knowledge required for this advanced electrical contractor classification. The course supports preparation for candidates pursuing North Carolina’s broadest regular electrical contractor license. The Unlimited classification permits a properly licensed contractor to perform electrical contracting projects without a project-value limitation, subject to applicable licensing laws, electrical codes, permitting requirements, inspections, safety standards, and professional responsibilities. Course preparation is based on the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 Edition; NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, 2019 Edition; Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, General Statutes Chapter 87, Article 4; the Board’s Rules for the Implementation of the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, Title 21, North Carolina Administrative Code, Chapter 18B; and the NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical Edition. No books are included with this online exam prep course. Students must obtain the required references separately. Using the same editions during preparation helps candidates become familiar with article locations, chapter layouts, tables, definitions, exceptions, indexes, and cross-references before the examination. The course is structured to support review of services, feeders, branch circuits, motors, transformers, generators, grounding, bonding, raceways, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, fire alarm systems, emergency systems, load calculations, voltage drop, electrical plans, contractor licensing law, Board rules, estimating, financial management, safety, and project administration. Unlimited electrical projects may involve large commercial services, industrial distribution systems, switchboards, panelboards, transformers, generators, motor loads, emergency power, fire alarm systems, special occupancies, renewable energy equipment, and extensive lighting and power plans. Candidates must be able to identify the governing Code requirement, locate it efficiently, perform required calculations, and apply the result to a realistic installation. The North Carolina Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination is open book for the approved technical references. The course includes preparation involving the 2020 NEC and NFPA 72, 2019 Edition. The licensing law, Board rules, and NASCLA business reference are used as closed-book study materials because those books are not allowed in the examination room. This online exam prep course helps candidates organize a broad examination into manageable technical and business subjects. It emphasizes consistent study, reference navigation, calculation practice, trade-focused review, and a clear understanding of the responsibilities associated with North Carolina electrical contracting. What You Get Online Exam Preparation: Structured review for the North Carolina PSI Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination. NEC Preparation: Study guidance based on the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 Edition. Fire Alarm Preparation: Review based on NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, 2019 Edition. Calculation Review: Preparation involving services, feeders, conductors, motors, transformers, grounding, raceways, boxes, loads, and voltage drop. Plan-Reading Preparation: Guidance for working with lighting plans, power plans, panel schedules, riser diagrams, symbols, equipment information, and installation notes. Licensing Review: Study support involving North Carolina electrical contractor law, Board rules, Unlimited qualifications, listed qualified individuals, and license operation. Business Review: Preparation involving contracts, estimating, bidding, scheduling, accounting, employment practices, safety, insurance, and project administration. No Books Included: All required Code books, licensing references, business references, and plans must be obtained separately. Exam Details The North Carolina Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination contains 100 multiple-choice questions. Candidates have a maximum of six hours to complete the examination, and a minimum score of 70 percent is required to pass. The examination is administered by PSI after the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors approves the applicant. Candidates must apply to the Board, document their qualifications, receive examination authorization, and then schedule their testing appointment through PSI. The Unlimited examination evaluates the technical, supervisory, licensing, business, and plan-reading knowledge needed to direct electrical contracting projects without a project-value limitation. Service and feeder preparation may include dwelling and commercial load calculations, service conductor sizing, service disconnects, grounding electrode conductors, neutral loads, parallel conductors, feeder demand factors, transformer secondaries, voltage drop, and protection of conductors and equipment. Branch-circuit preparation should include conductor ampacity, continuous and noncontinuous loads, receptacle loads, lighting loads, appliance circuits, multiwire branch circuits, conductor identification, overcurrent protection, voltage limitations, and requirements for specific occupancies. Motor preparation may involve full-load current, conductor sizing, feeder sizing, overload protection, short-circuit and ground-fault protection, controllers, disconnects, duty ratings, multimotor installations, and the correct use of NEC motor tables. Transformer preparation may include primary and secondary conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, separately derived systems, secondary-system calculations, ventilation, accessibility, clearances, and transformer installations within buildings. Grounding and bonding preparation should include grounding electrode systems, service bonding, separately derived systems, equipment grounding conductors, bonding jumpers, raceway bonding, structural metal, metal piping, objectionable current, and effective ground-fault current paths. Raceway and conductor questions may address raceway fill, conductor adjustment, ambient-temperature correction, terminal limitations, conductor insulation, physical protection, support, bends, cable trays, underground installations, pull boxes, junction boxes, and conductor-pulling requirements. Overcurrent-protection preparation may include standard fuse and circuit-breaker ratings, conductor protection, transformer protection, tap conductors, motor circuits, selective coordination, interrupting ratings, series ratings, equipment protection, and permitted exceptions. Special-system preparation may involve emergency systems, legally required standby systems, optional standby systems, generators, fire pumps, healthcare facilities, hazardous locations, marinas, swimming pools, photovoltaic systems, energy storage systems, and electric vehicle charging equipment. Fire alarm preparation may include fire alarm control units, initiating devices, notification appliances, supervising stations, emergency communications, signaling line circuits, notification appliance circuits, system power supplies, batteries, inspection, testing, maintenance, and documentation. Plan-reading preparation may involve lighting plans, power plans, one-line diagrams, riser diagrams, panel schedules, symbols, feeder routes, conductor callouts, motor connections, equipment ratings, installation notes, and specifications. Candidates should practice connecting information shown on a plan to the applicable NEC requirement. Business and law preparation may involve contracts, estimating, bidding, project scheduling, financial controls, employment practices, insurance, safety programs, recordkeeping, permits, inspections, license use, supervision, and the responsibilities of the listed qualified individual. Open Book Test The North Carolina Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates may use the approved 2020 National Electrical Code and NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, 2019 Edition, during the examination. The 2020 NEC supports examination questions involving electrical installations, calculations, services, feeders, branch circuits, motors, transformers, generators, grounding, bonding, conductor sizing, raceways, overcurrent protection, emergency systems, special occupancies, and special equipment. NFPA 72, 2019 Edition, supports preparation involving fire alarm fundamentals, initiating devices, notification appliances, supervising stations, emergency communications, pathways, system power, inspection, testing, maintenance, and documentation. The Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, Board rules, and NASCLA business reference are part of the course study material but are not permitted in the examination room. Candidates should study these subjects until they can answer licensing and business questions without relying on the books during the test. This course does not include the 2020 NEC, NFPA 72, licensing law, Board rules, NASCLA business reference, or lighting and power plans. Candidates are responsible for obtaining the references and materials needed for study and test-day use. Approved exam-room references must comply with current rules involving binding, highlighting, notes, tabs, and added materials. Candidates should review the current testing requirements before taking books to the PSI examination center. Open-book testing does not eliminate the need to understand the material. Candidates must know which reference applies, where the subject is located, how exceptions affect the general rule, and which values must be used in a calculation. A motor-feeder problem may require several NEC sections and tables. A transformer problem may involve primary protection, secondary conductors, grounding, bonding, and separately derived system provisions. A fire alarm question may require both the NEC and NFPA 72. Reference-navigation practice should include the index, table of contents, definitions, article and chapter layouts, tables, annex material, exceptions, and cross-references. The goal is to move directly to the relevant provision instead of searching through unrelated material. Timed practice is essential for a 100-question examination. Candidates should develop a consistent process: identify the topic, choose the proper reference, locate the governing rule, review the complete provision, check exceptions, perform the calculation, and select the best answer. Licensing Steps Review the Unlimited classification. Understand the authority, qualifications, financial responsibilities, and supervisory obligations associated with the license. Document qualifying experience. Gather employment records, project information, and experience statements showing the required electrical experience. Obtain supervisory statements. Secure statements from individuals familiar with the applicant’s ability to supervise and direct electrical wiring and installation work. Complete the examination application. Provide the personal, employment, experience, and background information requested by the Board. Submit supporting documentation. Include experience verification, supervisory statements, character references, and other required materials. Submit the examination fee. Include the applicable payment with the completed application. Receive Board approval. The Board reviews the application and determines whether the candidate meets the Unlimited examination qualifications. Receive examination authorization. Approved candidates receive information needed to register and schedule with PSI. Schedule the PSI examination. Select an available testing appointment within the authorized examination period. Obtain the required references. Purchase or otherwise obtain the approved technical books, closed-book study references, and required plans separately. Complete the online course. Work through the technical, calculation, plan-reading, licensing, and business subjects in an organized sequence. Practice reference navigation. Use the same approved technical references that will be taken to the examination center. Complete the examination. Bring the required identification and permitted materials to the PSI testing center. Complete the licensing process. After passing, satisfy the Board’s remaining business, financial, and listed qualified individual requirements. Maintain the license. Follow current renewal, continuing education, financial responsibility, supervision, and compliance requirements. State Requirements The North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors regulates the Unlimited examination and licensing process. The Board establishes applicant qualifications, reviews experience, authorizes candidates, certifies qualified individuals, issues licenses, and enforces electrical contracting laws and rules. An applicant for the Unlimited classification must document at least 9,000 hours of qualifying experience. At least 8,000 hours must be primary experience. The remaining experience may consist of primary experience, secondary experience, or a combination of both. Primary experience generally involves direct work installing electrical wiring and equipment governed by the NEC or work activities directly related to those installations. Recognized experience may also include qualifying supervisory, estimating, inspection, engineering, instructional, maintenance, military, and other approved electrical work. Unlimited applicants must provide statements from people familiar with their electrical experience and ability to supervise and direct electrical wiring and installation work. The Unlimited license permits electrical contracting projects regardless of project value. Unlike the Limited and Intermediate classifications, it does not impose a maximum dollar value on an individual electrical contracting project. The lack of a project-value ceiling does not remove the obligation to comply with the National Electrical Code, state construction requirements, permits, inspections, occupational safety rules, contract terms, and other laws governing electrical work. Electrical contracting must be conducted in the exact name shown on the active license. The licensed entity must maintain a listed qualified individual who is regularly on active duty and has the authority and responsibility to supervise and direct the electrical contracting performed under the license. Applicants for an Unlimited license must provide the financial responsibility or bonding documentation required by the Board. The documentation must relate to the license applicant and satisfy the requirements for the Unlimited classification. Passing the examination establishes the individual’s examination qualification but does not independently authorize electrical contracting. The appropriate license must be issued and active before regulated electrical work is offered or performed. License holders must continue complying with Board requirements after licensing. Misuse of a license, false advertising, fraud, misrepresentation, gross negligence, or unlicensed contracting may lead to disciplinary action. title: North Carolina Intermediate Electrical Contractor (I) - Online Exam Prep Course
description: North Carolina Intermediate Electrical Contractor (I) - Online Exam Prep Course Prepare for the North Carolina Intermediate Electrical Contractor examination with a focused online exam prep course designed to strengthen electrical code knowledge, reference navigation, calculation skills, plan-reading ability, and practical understanding of electrical contracting principles. The North Carolina Intermediate Electrical Contractor (I) - Online Exam Prep Course gives candidates an organized way to study the technical subjects associated with the Intermediate electrical contractor classification. Electrical contractor examinations require more than simply knowing electrical terminology. Candidates must be able to recognize applicable code requirements, interpret electrical installations, work through calculations, analyze plans and specifications, and efficiently locate information in technical reference materials. This course is structured to help students develop those skills through organized review and exam-oriented preparation. The course emphasizes study of the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 along with fire alarm concepts associated with NFPA 72. Candidates preparing for the Intermediate classification should develop familiarity with electrical systems, wiring methods, conductors, grounding and bonding, services, feeders, branch circuits, overcurrent protection, motors, transformers, equipment requirements, load calculations, and other electrical-code subjects relevant to contractor examination preparation. Because reference navigation is an important part of open-book electrical testing, effective preparation involves more than reading a code book from beginning to end. Students should learn how the NEC is organized, understand how articles and tables relate to one another, recognize commonly tested terminology, and practice finding applicable requirements efficiently. An organized preparation program can help candidates turn their field knowledge into a more effective exam-day strategy. This online course is suited for electricians, electrical professionals, qualified-individual candidates, and contractors preparing to pursue the North Carolina Intermediate electrical contractor classification. Whether you have extensive field experience or are returning to technical study after time away from formal testing, the goal is to create a structured preparation process that combines electrical knowledge with practical reference skills. Exam Details The North Carolina Intermediate Electrical Contractor examination is associated with the Intermediate electrical contracting classification administered through the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Candidates pursuing this classification must prepare for technical electrical subjects and the application of electrical-code requirements. North Carolina electrical contractor examinations evaluate knowledge relating to the safe and proper installation of electrical work and equipment. Examination preparation can include National Electrical Code provisions, analysis of electrical plans and specifications, electrical calculations, installation fundamentals, and other subjects associated with electrical contracting. Intermediate candidates should be prepared to work with electrical plans in addition to technical references. Plan-reading skills can require candidates to identify equipment, circuits, loads, electrical symbols, feeder arrangements, service information, and installation details. Understanding how information shown on a plan connects to NEC requirements is an important part of comprehensive electrical contractor exam preparation. Calculation skills should also be part of a candidate's study program. Electrical contractor preparation may involve conductor sizing, load calculations, overcurrent protection, service and feeder calculations, motors, transformers, voltage-related concepts, and other mathematical applications found throughout the NEC. Candidates should practice both identifying the correct calculation method and locating the code provisions or tables that support the calculation. Another important preparation area is learning how NEC rules interact. A question may require information from more than one article, definition, table, exception, or equipment requirement. Candidates who understand the organization of the code are generally better positioned to determine where to begin searching and how to confirm that a selected requirement applies to the situation described. Open Book Test The North Carolina electrical contractor examination is conducted as an open book test. Open-book testing makes reference navigation an essential exam skill. Candidates should not assume that simply having the permitted books available will eliminate the need for thorough preparation. Technical references contain extensive material, and searching for every answer from scratch can consume valuable examination time. Students should become familiar with the organization of their approved references before examination day. With the NEC, this includes becoming comfortable with the table of contents, index, articles, definitions, informational tables, conductor tables, grounding and bonding provisions, equipment requirements, and other frequently used sections. Reference materials brought into the testing center are subject to North Carolina examination rules. Candidates should review the current examination handbook and testing requirements before their scheduled examination so their books, tabs, markings, and other permitted materials comply with current rules. A useful study strategy is to practice answering a question before looking up the requirement and then confirm the answer directly in the applicable reference. When an answer is incorrect, return to the relevant article or section and identify why. Repeating this process helps build stronger code familiarity while improving the ability to recognize where information is located. Licensing Steps Candidates pursuing the North Carolina Intermediate electrical contractor classification should begin by reviewing the current requirements established by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. The examination is part of the broader qualification and licensing process, and passing an examination does not by itself complete every requirement associated with obtaining an electrical contracting license. The application process begins with selecting the appropriate electrical contractor classification and completing the examination application requirements established by the Board. Applicants should carefully review current eligibility requirements, experience documentation, application instructions, examination procedures, and supporting materials before submitting an application. Once an applicant is approved for examination, scheduling is handled through the Board's designated testing process. Candidates should follow the instructions provided with their examination approval and review applicable examination-center requirements before selecting and attending their test appointment. Preparation should begin well before the scheduled examination date. Candidates should organize their permitted references, review major NEC subject areas, practice electrical calculations, study plan-reading concepts, and work through exam-oriented material consistently instead of relying on last-minute review. After completing the examination, candidates pursuing licensure must continue following the Board's requirements for their classification. Examination success and license issuance are separate parts of the process, so applicants should make sure all required licensing conditions are completed according to current North Carolina rules. State Requirements North Carolina regulates electrical contracting through the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Applicants for certification as a qualified individual must satisfy requirements established by state law and Board rules, including applicable experience and examination requirements. The Intermediate classification is intended for electrical contractors working within the scope and limitations established for that classification under North Carolina law and Board rules. Candidates should review the current classification requirements before applying so they understand the experience standards, project limitations, application obligations, and licensing responsibilities associated with the Intermediate license. Electrical contractor licensing is designed to help protect public life, health, and property by requiring qualified individuals to demonstrate technical and practical knowledge concerning electrical installations. For an Intermediate candidate, exam preparation should therefore focus on understanding electrical requirements rather than memorizing isolated answers. Field experience is valuable, but candidates should remember that everyday workplace practices do not always substitute for the exact requirements contained in the NEC. Examination questions may depend on code definitions, specific limitations, exceptions, calculations, or table values. Studying the applicable references directly helps candidates distinguish between common field habits and code-based requirements. Reference Books National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020The National Electrical Code is a primary technical reference for electrical contractor examination preparation. Candidates should become familiar with its organization and provisions covering wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, equipment for general use, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, communications systems, tables, definitions, calculations, grounding and bonding, services, feeders, branch circuits, motors, transformers, and other electrical installation requirements. NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm CodeNFPA 72 addresses fire alarm and signaling system requirements. Candidates studying this reference should focus on understanding system concepts, installation requirements, signaling principles, initiating and notification equipment, and the organization of the standard so relevant provisions can be located efficiently during study and examination preparation. Test Information and Study Materials Successful preparation for the North Carolina Intermediate Electrical Contractor examination should combine technical review, reference navigation, calculations, plan analysis, and repeated application of electrical-code concepts. The online exam prep format provides candidates with a structured way to bring those areas together rather than studying individual subjects in isolation. Begin with the NEC. Become comfortable locating definitions and identifying which article governs a particular installation. Review commonly encountered areas such as services, feeders, branch circuits, conductors, ampacity, overcurrent protection, boxes, raceways, grounding and bonding, motors, transformers, equipment, special occupancies, and special systems. Understanding the structure of the NEC is often just as important as remembering an individual rule. Pay particular attention to tables and calculations. Electrical examinations frequently require candidates to recognize the correct table, apply adjustment or correction factors where applicable, determine conductor or equipment requirements, and perform calculations accurately. Instead of memorizing every numerical value, understand where values come from and how the applicable NEC rules direct the calculation. Grounding and bonding deserves concentrated study because it combines terminology, installation rules, conductor sizing, equipment requirements, and multiple related NEC sections. Candidates should be comfortable distinguishing grounding from bonding concepts and recognizing the different conductors and components involved in electrical grounding and bonding systems. Motors and transformers are additional areas where technical understanding and calculations come together. Students should practice identifying applicable rules, locating required tables, determining conductor requirements, and recognizing overcurrent or protection considerations associated with electrical equipment. Plan reading should also become part of regular study. Look at electrical drawings and practice identifying symbols, circuits, equipment, panel information, loads, feeder arrangements, and other information. Then connect those plans to the applicable code requirements. This helps develop the type of applied reasoning that contractor examinations can require. Fire alarm preparation should include familiarity with the organization of NFPA 72 and the ability to navigate the standard efficiently. Candidates should understand core fire alarm and signaling concepts and know where to search when a question involves system components or installation requirements. When reviewing missed questions, avoid memorizing only the correct answer. Find the underlying rule. That process builds transferable knowledge that can help with differently worded questions covering the same concept. Practice-oriented preparation also helps candidates identify weak areas early. When a calculation, code topic, or reference section causes difficulty, students can spend more time reviewing that subject instead of repeatedly studying material they already understand. 1 Exam Prep is designed to help students build a more confident study routine through organized review, reference navigation, technical preparation, and repeated application of electrical concepts. The goal is to help candidates arrive at examination day better prepared to work through code questions, calculations, plan-based information, and technical electrical scenarios. Is the North Carolina Intermediate Electrical Contractor exam open book? Yes. North Carolina electrical contractor examinations are open book, subject to the Board's rules regarding which references and materials may be taken into the testing center. What electrical code should I study? The course materials provided for this product identify the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 as a primary reference for preparation. Should I study NFPA 72 for the Intermediate exam? Yes. Fire alarm and signaling concepts contained in NFPA 72 are part of the reference-based preparation associated with the Intermediate electrical contractor examination. What NEC topics should I review? Important study areas include electrical definitions, services, feeders, branch circuits, conductor requirements, ampacity, wiring methods, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, motors, transformers, equipment requirements, special systems, calculations, and other applicable NEC provisions. Do I need to practice electrical calculations? Yes. Electrical calculations are an important part of contractor exam preparation. Becoming familiar with NEC articles, tables, definitions, indexes, and related sections can reduce the amount of time spent searching during the test. Should I study electrical plans? Yes. title: North Carolina 2026 Journeyman Electrician Exam Prep and Study Guide: 12 Practice Exams +2 Full Final Exams: Trusted by 50k Electricians
description: North Carolina 2026 Journeyman Electrician Exam Prep and Study Guide: 12 Practice Exams + 2 Full Final Exams: Trusted by 50k Electricians When electricians talk about “the North Carolina journeyman exam,” what they’re usually describing is the real-world, code-based licensing test experience: a timed exam that measures how well you apply the NEC, how quickly you can navigate references, and how consistently you can make the right call under pressure. In North Carolina, statewide electrical licensing is handled through the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors (NCBEEC) for electrical contracting licenses (Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, and Special Restricted classifications) administered through PSI. The NCBEEC exam handbook makes it clear that these are open-book examinations, and that candidates are expected to bring specified references into the exam center. This North Carolina 2026 Journeyman Electrician Exam Prep and Study Guide is built to help you train for that exam-day reality with a practice-first approach. You’ll get 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams designed to sharpen the skills that most often decide pass/fail: Fast navigation: getting to the right code section or table without losing minutes. Clean accuracy: reducing misses caused by misreads, missed exceptions, or rushed math. Steady pacing: keeping momentum so one time-sink question doesn’t derail your entire score. Trusted by 50k electricians reflects what consistently works in trade testing: repetition. Practice exams turn studying into performance training. Instead of reading and hoping it sticks, you train the same workflow you’ll use in the testing center: read the scenario, identify the topic, confirm the rule efficiently, answer, move on. Repeat that enough times, and your test-day confidence becomes something you can feel because you earned it through reps. Exam Details The NCBEEC Examination Information Handbook (administered through PSI) describes exam classifications and testing structure for North Carolina electrical contracting licenses. According to the handbook: Limited / Intermediate / Unlimited classifications: the exam consists of 100 multiple-choice questions with a maximum time of 6 hours. Special Restricted classifications (excluding certain categories): 40 multiple-choice questions with a maximum time of 3 hours. Special Restricted Fire Alarm/Low Voltage (FA/LV): 50 multiple-choice questions with a maximum time of 3 hours. Special Restricted Swimming Pool Bonding (SP-SP): 25 multiple-choice questions with a maximum time of 1 hour. Regardless of classification, the common denominator is performance under time pressure. Your exam score depends on how well you can apply code requirements to realistic installation and safety scenarios, then keep moving. This study guide’s practice-first structure is designed to build that exact exam-day skill set. Open Book Test Yes—North Carolina NCBEEC examinations are open book. The NCBEEC handbook states: “The examinations are OPEN BOOK,” and it explains that candidates must bring required references to the exam center, with strict rules on what is allowed in those books. Open book is a major advantage only if you train correctly. The exam is not designed for you to slowly look up every answer. It rewards the electrician who can confirm details quickly and keep moving. North Carolina’s handbook includes reference-handling rules that should shape how you prepare and how you practice: Bring your own references: candidates are responsible for bringing their own references to the examination center. Binding rules: references must be softbound, spiral, or hardbound; loose leaf references are not allowed. Preparation before test day: references may be highlighted, underlined, and/or annotated prior to the exam session (notes are allowed under the handbook’s rules). No writing during the exam: references may not be written in during the examination session. No extra papers: additional papers (loose or attached) are not permitted within the references. Tabs: permanent tabs only; temporary tabs such as Post-it notes or stapled tabs must be removed before the exam begins. Very important: the handbook also explains that some exam content is treated as closed book content. It notes that questions concerning the licensing law, Board rules, and the NASCLA business/law/project management reference are “CLOSED BOOK” questions (no candidate is allowed to refer to those documents during the exam). That means the best prep plan is balanced: strong open-book speed for code questions, plus familiarity with the administrative/business content so those questions don’t slow you down. This study guide is designed to strengthen open-book speed and accuracy through repetition, while also reinforcing the exam habits that protect your score: careful reading, smart pacing, and consistent decision-making. Licensing Steps North Carolina’s state-level electrical licensing for contractors follows a clear exam authorization and scheduling flow described in the NCBEEC handbook. A practical timeline looks like this: Choose your classification: Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, or an applicable Special Restricted classification. Submit your exam application to NCBEEC: the handbook instructs candidates to complete the exam application form and submit required documentation and fees as detailed in the application instructions. Receive a Notice of Approval: if approved, NCBEEC issues an approval letter with your authorization period. Watch for PSI eligibility confirmation: the handbook explains PSI sends an email notifying you that you are eligible to test. Register and schedule with PSI: the handbook states you can register by phone or online through PSI once eligible. Test within your authorization window: the handbook states you can register for your approved exam once within your 90-day authorization period. This prep product supports the step you control most: being ready to perform when your authorization window opens. Practice exams help you build a repeatable method so you’re not “searching your way” through the code on test day. State Requirements North Carolina’s state electrical licensing (as described by the NCBEEC handbook) is focused on licensing electrical contractors in the Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited classifications, as well as several Special Restricted classifications administered through the Board’s exam program. Because licensing eligibility and documentation requirements depend on the classification and the Board’s application rules, the smartest approach is to align your application path with your intended classification and then prepare for the exam as a performance test. This guide is built around the most transferable exam requirements across North Carolina’s open-book electrical testing experience: Code-based decision-making: interpreting scenarios and selecting the correct NEC requirement. Reference navigation: using the index, table of contents, and key terms efficiently. Time management: maintaining pace across an exam-length sitting. Detail discipline: catching exceptions, definitions, and conditions that flip the correct answer. Reference Books National Electrical Code (NEC), 2020 editionThe NCBEEC handbook states each candidate is required to bring their own copy of the 2020 NEC to the exam center. National Fire Alarm Code, 2013 editionThe NCBEEC handbook states candidates in certain classifications (including Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, SP-SFD, and SP-FA/LV) are required to bring a copy of the 2013 National Fire Alarm Code. The handbook also notes that the exam includes questions concerning North Carolina licensing law, Board rules, and a NASCLA business/law/project management reference, and it states those are treated as closed book questions during the exam. Test Information and Study Materials Timed exams reward performance. The fastest way to improve performance is to practice the same job the exam demands—then review what you missed until you stop missing it. That’s why this guide includes 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams: enough repetition to build real momentum and measurable improvement. Use the exams in a score-building progression: Phase 1: Baseline + weak-area map (Practice Exams 1–4). Take your first practice exams at a steady pace. Track what you miss and what slows you down. Don’t just mark “wrong”—label why: misread wording, missed exception, slow lookup, wrong table, rushed math, or uncertainty about the tested topic. Phase 2: Build your open-book rhythm (Practice Exams 5–8). Tighten your method. For each question: identify the topic → go to the most likely code location → confirm the controlling requirement → answer → move on. Your goal is fewer “wandering searches.” Phase 3: Train pacing under pressure (Practice Exams 9–12). Add realistic timing pressure. Practice protecting the clock. Learn when to confirm quickly, when to answer from understanding, and when to move forward instead of getting trapped. Phase 4: Prove readiness (2 Full Final Exams). Treat the finals like your dress rehearsal: one sitting, timed, distraction-free. Review every missed question and fix patterns before your scheduled test date. The review routine that raises scores: Find the controlling section/table for every missed question and read it carefully (especially exceptions and definitions). Redo the lookup until you can find the answer quickly and confidently. Label the miss pattern so you stop repeating it (misread, missed exception, slow search, wrong table, rushed calculation). Retest soon so the correction becomes a habit. Where candidates often gain points fastest: Wiring methods and materials: questions often hinge on one condition. Practice reduces detail-based misses. Branch circuits and conductors: speed improves when you recognize which code areas and tables are most likely in play. Grounding and bonding: repetition helps you catch the conditions and exceptions that change the answer. Overcurrent protection and equipment rules: disciplined confirmation prevents avoidable errors. Fire alarm / low voltage topics (when applicable): practice prevents surprises and keeps you from overthinking. The goal is simple: by the time you reach the final exams, the test should feel familiar—familiar pacing, familiar workflow, and a strategy you trust. How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal 1 Exam Prep supports North Carolina electrician candidates with preparation that’s structured, practical, and focused on exam performance. You already have trade knowledge—this guide helps you demonstrate it under the conditions the exam creates: timed questions, open-book navigation, and detail-sensitive wording. Organized study guidance: a clear practice-and-review routine so you always know what to do next. Trade-focused review: reinforces applied understanding and code-based decision-making. Practice-oriented preparation: repeated exams build speed, accuracy, and pacing together. Reference navigation habits: open-book skill improves through repetition and intentional lookups. Confidence-building structure: full exam simulations reduce surprises and help you stay calm on test day. This is prep built for working electricians: practice like the exam, review what you miss, correct the pattern, repeat—then rehearse with full finals so you’re ready to perform. FAQ Section Is the North Carolina electrical exam open book? Yes. The NCBEEC examination handbook states the examinations are open book and describes the required references and rules for tabs, markings, and prohibited materials. How many questions and how much time should I plan for? The NCBEEC handbook lists 100 questions with a 6-hour maximum for Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited classifications. It also lists different question counts and time limits for Special Restricted classifications. Do I bring my own codebooks to the testing center? Yes. The NCBEEC handbook states candidates are responsible for bringing their own references and identifies the 2020 NEC as required. Are all exam questions open book? No. The NCBEEC handbook explains that some content (including licensing law, Board rules, and the NASCLA business/law/project management reference) is treated as closed book questions during the exam. Can I tab and highlight my NEC? Yes, within the handbook’s rules. The NCBEEC handbook allows highlighting and notes prepared before the exam and allows permanent tabs, while prohibiting temporary tabs like Post-it notes. How should I use the 2 full final exams? Use them near the end of your prep as full dress rehearsals. Take each final timed and uninterrupted, then review every missed question and retest the topics that cost you points. How many practice exams are included? This study guide includes 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams designed to help you build speed, accuracy, and pacing through realistic repetition. Does this guide guarantee I will pass? No. Results depend on your preparation, experience, and test-day performance. This guide is designed to make your prep more effective by improving open-book navigation, accuracy, and pacing through realistic practice and structured review. Where can I find more electrician exam prep? You can find additional electrician exam prep resources at 1examprep.com.
