title: North Carolina Contractor License Application Service
description: North Carolina Contractor License Application Service The North Carolina Contractor License Application Service is designed for contractors, construction business owners, and qualifying parties who want organized support while preparing a North Carolina general contractor license application. North Carolina contractor licensing is handled by the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors, commonly known as NCLBGC. The application process can involve selecting the correct classification, choosing the proper license limitation, identifying a qualifying party, preparing financial information, completing background-related requirements, receiving exam eligibility, scheduling examinations through PSI, and submitting supporting documents before a license can be issued. North Carolina requires a general contractor license for contractors who bid on, contract for, construct, manage, or superintend certain construction work when the project cost meets the state licensing threshold. The correct application path depends on the type of work being performed, the classification requested, the license limitation selected, the financial information provided, and the qualifying party connected to the application. This service helps applicants approach the North Carolina licensing process with a clearer plan. Instead of trying to sort through NCLBGC classifications, license limitations, online application requirements, financial responsibility documents, PSI testing instructions, qualifying party rules, local permit questions, and trade-board requirements alone, applicants receive structured guidance focused on preparing a cleaner and more organized application package. The goal is to help contractors understand what the board is asking for and gather the information needed before submission. The North Carolina Contractor License Application Service is helpful for first-time applicants, out-of-state contractors expanding into North Carolina, businesses applying for a general contractor license, contractors changing or adding classifications, companies reviewing limitation levels, and individuals serving as qualifying parties. It is also useful for contractors who understand construction work but want support with the administrative side of licensing. North Carolina contractor licensing is not only about passing an exam. Applicants must choose the correct classification and limitation, satisfy application requirements, provide evidence of financial responsibility, identify a qualifying party, complete any required background process, pass the required examination or document an accepted exam transfer when applicable, and maintain compliance after the license is issued. This application service does not replace NCLBGC, does not guarantee approval, does not include state or PSI fees, and does not waive any North Carolina licensing, examination, financial, background, classification, limitation, local permit, insurance, business, or trade requirement. 1 Exam Prep helps applicants prepare, organize, and approach the application process with a more professional workflow. What You Get Application Guidance: Support understanding the North Carolina contractor license application path based on the work your business plans to perform. Classification Review: Help organizing the application around the proper North Carolina general contractor classification, such as building, residential, highway, public utilities, or specialty work. License Limitation Planning: Guidance reviewing Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited license limitation levels and organizing the application around the level requested. Qualifying Party Support: Help organizing information for the individual who will qualify the license by meeting board requirements and passing the required examination when applicable. Financial Document Planning: Support organizing financial responsibility information connected to the license limitation requested. Form Organization: Assistance reviewing application structure and gathering business, ownership, contact, responsible-party, and qualifying-party information before submission. Exam Workflow Support: Guidance understanding where NCLBGC eligibility review, PSI scheduling, examination requirements, and final board review fit into the licensing process. Trade and Local Requirement Planning: Support recognizing when electrical, plumbing, mechanical, fire sprinkler, local permits, or other separate requirements may apply. Submission Preparation: Support preparing a cleaner and more organized application package before the applicant submits materials to the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. Follow-Up Support Structure: Guidance on tracking submitted materials and organizing responses if the board requests corrections, clarification, or additional documentation. Exam Details North Carolina general contractor examinations are administered through PSI after the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors determines that the applicant is eligible to test. Applicants must submit the required application materials and receive board approval before scheduling the examination. PSI provides the exam scheduling and testing process after eligibility is granted. Applicants are required to qualify the license through an approved qualifying party. The qualifying party is the individual connected to the license who satisfies the examination requirement for the classification. Depending on the applicant’s situation, the qualifying party may be an owner, officer, member, managing employee, or other person accepted by the board as the qualifier for the license. North Carolina general contractor classifications include Building, Residential, Highway, Public Utilities, and Specialty classifications. The classification should match the work the contractor intends to bid, contract for, construct, manage, or superintend. Applicants should not choose a classification based only on preference; the classification should reflect the actual scope of work the business plans to perform. North Carolina also uses license limitations. A Limited license allows the licensee to act as general contractor for a single project up to the dollar limit allowed for that limitation. An Intermediate license allows work on a single project up to a higher limit. An Unlimited license does not place the same project-value cap on the license. The limitation requested must be supported by the financial responsibility information required by the board. The North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors accepts the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors for the Building classification. NASCLA is administered separately from the North Carolina PSI examination program. Applicants using a NASCLA exam path should still follow NCLBGC application instructions because board approval, classification, limitation, financial responsibility, and final license issuance requirements still apply. The North Carolina Contractor License Application Service is not an exam-preparation course. Its purpose is application support. When an exam is required, this service helps organize that requirement within the larger licensing plan so applicants understand where testing fits into the process. Exam-prep books, courses, practice tests, and study materials are separate products when available. Open Book Test North Carolina general contractor examinations administered through PSI are open-book examinations for exams that list approved reference materials. Candidates must follow the current PSI Candidate Information Bulletin for the exact references allowed for the examination they are approved to take. Approved references may be used only according to PSI rules. Candidates should review the current bulletin before test day so books, tabs, highlighting, and other reference materials follow testing requirements. Unauthorized notes, loose papers, unapproved references, or materials that do not comply with PSI rules may be rejected at the testing center. Open-book testing does not mean the exam is easy. Applicants still need to understand how to navigate the approved references quickly, apply business and construction knowledge, manage time, and answer questions tied to the classification being tested. Strong preparation should include reference navigation, practice questions, content-outline review, and organized study planning. Licensing Steps The first step in the North Carolina contractor licensing process is identifying whether the work requires a general contractor license. Contractors should review the project value, work scope, and role they will perform. Work involving construction, management, or supervision of buildings, highways, public utilities, grading, or other improvements may require a license when the project meets the state threshold. The next step is choosing the correct classification. North Carolina classifications include Building, Residential, Highway, Public Utilities, and Specialty classifications. Specialty classifications may apply to specific types of work, while broader classifications may apply to larger scopes. The classification selected should match the work the contractor intends to perform. After the classification is selected, the applicant should choose the proper limitation level. North Carolina uses Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited limitations. The limitation affects the size of projects the licensee may contract for under the license. Applicants should choose a limitation that matches their business goals and the financial responsibility documentation they can support. The applicant must then identify the qualifying party. The qualifying party is the person who satisfies the examination requirement for the license classification. This person must be properly connected to the applicant and should be prepared to complete the required exam workflow if an exam has not already been accepted by the board. The applicant should organize business information before starting the application. Common application items may include the legal business name, trade name when applicable, business entity type, ownership information, corporate officer or member information, mailing address, physical address, phone number, email address, and responsible-party details. The business name used on the application should match supporting business records. Financial responsibility information should be prepared carefully. The board requires evidence of financial responsibility, and the documentation required depends on the limitation requested. Applicants should organize financial statements, balance information, or other documents required by the board for the license level being requested. Applicants should also prepare for background-related requirements. The board may require consent to a criminal background check as part of the licensing process. Disclosure questions and background-related forms should be answered accurately and supported with documents when requested. Once the application is submitted and the board determines eligibility, the qualifying party follows the PSI scheduling process for the required examination. Applicants should schedule only the examination tied to the approved classification or accepted exam path. After the exam requirement is satisfied and all application materials are complete, the board reviews the application for final license issuance. State Requirements North Carolina general contractor licenses are issued by the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. The board regulates general contractor licensing for covered work and provides application, classification, limitation, examination, renewal, and compliance requirements. A Building Classification applies to building construction and related work within the scope authorized by the board. Applicants seeking this classification should review the board’s classification language and make sure the work they plan to perform fits the classification. A Residential Classification applies to residential construction work within the scope authorized by the board. Contractors focusing on residential construction should review whether this classification matches their planned work. A Highway Classification applies to highway construction and related work within the scope authorized by the board. Applicants should select this path only when the work fits the highway classification. A Public Utilities Classification applies to public utilities construction work within the scope authorized by the board. Applicants should review utility-related work carefully before selecting this classification. A Specialty Classification applies to specific types of construction work recognized by the board. Specialty applicants should make sure the selected specialty matches the actual work the business plans to perform. License Limitations determine the size of projects a contractor may perform. North Carolina uses Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited limitations. The limitation requested must be supported by financial responsibility information required by the board. Qualifying Party Requirements are central to the application. The qualifying party must satisfy the examination requirement for the classification and must be properly connected to the applicant. If the qualifying party leaves the license, the licensee must address that change according to board rules. Separate Trade Requirements may also apply. Electrical, plumbing, HVAC, fire sprinkler, and certain other regulated work may require separate state trade credentials. A general contractor license does not replace a required trade license when state trade law requires one. Local Permits and Inspections may still apply. Even after a North Carolina general contractor license is issued, specific projects may require local building permits, trade permits, plan review, zoning approval, inspections, or other local approval before work begins. State fees, application fees, PSI examination fees, license fees, renewal fees, insurance costs, bond costs when applicable, financial document costs, business registration fees, permit fees, and other government or third-party charges are separate from this application service unless a product listing clearly states otherwise. Applicants should be prepared to pay required fees directly to the proper agency, testing provider, municipality, insurer, financial professional, or other authority. Test Information and Study Materials North Carolina contractor applicants should use study materials that match the exact classification and exam path approved by the board. A Building applicant may need different preparation than a Residential, Highway, Public Utilities, or Specialty applicant. Applicants using the NASCLA path should follow NASCLA’s examination instructions and the board’s rules for accepting that exam for the Building classification. The exam content may include business law, project management, construction administration, safety, plan reading, estimating, code knowledge, trade-specific knowledge, and classification-related topics. The exact content depends on the examination approved for the applicant’s classification. Because the PSI-administered North Carolina contractor exams are open book, applicants should prepare by learning how to use the approved references efficiently. Good preparation includes tabbing and highlighting within allowed rules, practicing timed questions, reviewing content outlines, and learning where common topics are located in the approved materials. Applicants should not assume that a book list for one classification applies to every North Carolina contractor exam. The current PSI Candidate Information Bulletin identifies references and testing rules for each examination. Applicants should rely on the bulletin tied to the exam they are authorized to take. This application service helps applicants organize the licensing paperwork that surrounds the exam process. For applicants who also need exam preparation, separate study products may be useful. Those products should match the North Carolina exam, classification, limitation, and approved reference list connected to the applicant’s license path. The North Carolina contractor application process can feel detailed because it may involve classification selection, limitation planning, qualifying party information, financial responsibility documents, background requirements, PSI examination workflow, NASCLA exam transfer questions, local permit requirements, and final board review. This service helps organize those pieces so applicants can move forward with a clearer plan. Our team helps applicants review the likely license path, organize application information, prepare common supporting documents, understand qualifying party requirements, and plan for the exam and final application workflow. This can be especially useful for contractors who are experienced in construction but unfamiliar with North Carolina’s licensing paperwork. 1 Exam Prep supports applicants through practical application guidance rather than unrealistic promises. We help create a more organized workflow, explain how the application pieces fit together, and support applicants as they prepare to submit licensing materials. When exam preparation is needed, applicants can use separate exam-prep resources to prepare for the testing stage. This service does not guarantee license approval, exam results, faster processing, board acceptance, or any state decision. NCLBGC controls application review and final licensing decisions. 1 Exam Prep’s role is to support applicants with organized preparation, licensing guidance, document planning, and confidence-building structure throughout the application process. What is the North Carolina Contractor License Application Service? The North Carolina Contractor License Application Service is a professional application support service that helps contractors prepare and organize a North Carolina general contractor license application. It focuses on classification review, limitation planning, qualifying party workflow, form organization, document planning, exam workflow support, and submission preparation. Who issues North Carolina general contractor licenses? North Carolina general contractor licenses are issued by the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. When is a North Carolina general contractor license required? A North Carolina general contractor license is required for covered construction work when the project meets the state licensing threshold. Contractors should review the work scope, project value, and role they will perform before bidding, contracting, managing, or supervising construction work. What are the North Carolina general contractor classifications? The classification should match the work the contractor intends to perform. What are North Carolina contractor license limitations? North Carolina uses Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited license limitations. The limitation affects the size of projects the licensee may contract for and must be supported by financial responsibility documentation. Do North Carolina contractor applicants need board approval before taking the exam? Yes. Applicants must submit the required application materials to the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. The board determines exam eligibility before the qualifying party schedules the required exam through PSI. Are North Carolina contractor exams open book? Yes. PSI-administered North Carolina general contractor exams are open book for examinations that list approved references. Candidates must follow the current PSI Candidate Information Bulletin for the exact reference list and testing rules. Does North Carolina accept the NASCLA exam? Applicants must still satisfy board application, classification, limitation, and final approval requirements. Does this service include exam preparation? No. This product is an application service. Does this service include the fee paid to the state? No. State fees are not included in the North Carolina Contractor License Application Service. Application fees, PSI examination fees, licensing fees, renewal fees, financial document costs, permit fees, insurance costs, and other government or third-party charges are separate. Can 1 Exam Prep guarantee that my North Carolina contractor license will be approved? No. License approval is controlled by the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. This service helps applicants prepare and organize the application package, but it does not guarantee approval, processing time, exam results, or any state or local decision. title: North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor Exam Book Package
description: North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor Exam Book Package Prepare for the North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor examination with a focused collection of North Carolina code books, administrative requirements, and licensing rules. This exam book package brings together the listed references used to study fuel-gas piping systems, mechanical installations, residential construction requirements, code administration, inspections, permitting, and the laws and rules enforced by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Plumbing, Heating, and Fire Sprinkler Contractors. Fuel piping work requires more than knowing how to connect pipe and equipment. A qualified contractor must understand how fuel piping systems are designed, installed, supported, tested, protected, inspected, and placed into service. Contractors must also know how fuel piping requirements interact with mechanical systems, residential construction provisions, combustion-air requirements, appliance locations, venting systems, building-code administration, and state licensing responsibilities. The North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor Exam Book Package is designed to help candidates organize their preparation around the primary references listed for this examination. The collection includes the North Carolina Administrative Code and Policies, North Carolina Fuel Gas Code, North Carolina Mechanical Code, North Carolina Residential Code, and the North Carolina Board’s current Laws & Rules publication. Each book serves a distinct purpose during preparation. The North Carolina Fuel Gas Code addresses fuel-gas piping systems, appliances, combustion air, venting, sizing, installation, testing, and related safety provisions. The North Carolina Mechanical Code supports questions involving mechanical equipment, ventilation, combustion systems, ducts, exhaust, equipment clearances, and associated installation requirements. The North Carolina Residential Code addresses fuel-gas and mechanical work in one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses within its scope. The North Carolina Administrative Code and Policies reference supports study of code administration, enforcement procedures, permits, inspections, interpretations, responsibilities, and other statewide construction-code policies. The Board’s Laws & Rules publication focuses on licensing authority, classifications, examinations, contractor responsibilities, supervision, business practices, disciplinary provisions, and the regulations governing licensed plumbing, heating, fuel piping, and fire sprinkler professionals. This package also supports open-book exam preparation. Open-book testing rewards candidates who know both the subject matter and the organization of their references. Successful preparation involves learning which book applies to a question, identifying effective search terms, locating the correct chapter or section, and confirming the answer without losing unnecessary time. What You Get North Carolina Administration Code and Policies, 2018 Edition North Carolina Fuel Gas Code, 2018 Edition North Carolina Mechanical Code, 2018 Edition North Carolina Residential Code, 2018 Edition NC Board's Laws & Rules – 2026 Edition Exam Details The North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor examination is part of the licensing program administered by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Plumbing, Heating, and Fire Sprinkler Contractors. The Board regulates individuals and businesses performing plumbing, heating, fuel piping, and fire sprinkler contracting work within its statutory authority. North Carolina recognizes fuel piping as a regulated area of contracting. State rules provide that contracting or installing fuel piping extending from an approved fuel source at or near a premises to a point within the premises requires an appropriate plumbing, heating, or fuel piping license. The applicable license depends on the work being performed and the classification held by the contractor. The examination evaluates a candidate’s ability to locate, interpret, and apply North Carolina code requirements and Board regulations. Study areas represented by the books in this package include fuel-gas piping materials, pipe sizing, pressure limitations, system testing, appliance connections, shutoff valves, regulators, sediment traps, combustion air, venting, equipment installation, residential provisions, inspections, permits, code administration, and licensing responsibilities. Questions may require candidates to identify a specific code provision, determine which requirement controls a field condition, distinguish between permitted and prohibited practices, or apply a rule to a practical installation scenario. Candidates should be prepared to move between multiple books because a single project may involve fuel-gas, mechanical, residential, administrative, and licensing requirements. The Board directs applicants to obtain the required reference materials before submitting an examination application. Candidates should review the current Board exam information, application instructions, and book-reference requirements when preparing to apply. Examination approval and licensing eligibility are determined through the Board’s established application process. Open Book Test The North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates are expected to bring the permitted reference books needed for their approved examination. Only materials allowed under the Board’s examination rules may be taken into the examination room. Open-book does not mean that every answer will be easy to find. The examination measures how well candidates understand the work and how effectively they can use the codes. A candidate who opens an unfamiliar book for the first time at the testing site may spend too much time searching through similar sections, exceptions, definitions, and cross-references. Begin by learning the structure of each reference. Review every table of contents, chapter title, index, appendix, definition section, and major subject heading. Identify where the books address piping materials, sizing tables, installation methods, testing, appliance connections, combustion air, venting, permits, inspections, and Board requirements. Practice selecting the correct book before searching for an answer. A question about pipe sizing, regulators, valves, or pressure testing will generally direct attention to the Fuel Gas Code. A question involving mechanical equipment, ventilation, exhaust, or system installation may require the Mechanical Code. Work within a dwelling may require the Residential Code, while questions about licensing, supervision, applications, or contractor conduct may require the Board’s Laws & Rules. The Board’s published examination-material requirements allow approved original reference books and specify how those books may be prepared. Commercially available permanent index tabs may be permitted, and highlighting may be allowed. Handwritten notes, added formulas, loose papers, unauthorized inserts, homemade tabs, and altered reference materials are restricted. Candidates should follow the current examination instructions exactly when preparing their books. A strong preparation method is to complete timed lookup exercises. Choose a topic, identify two or three likely index terms, locate the controlling section, read the main rule and its exceptions, and confirm the answer. Repeat the exercise across all books until the navigation process becomes familiar. Licensing Steps Determine the correct license category. Review the scope of the North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor license and confirm that it matches the work you intend to perform. Obtain the required reference books. The Board instructs applicants to have the necessary current code books and Board publications before submitting an application for examination. Document the required experience. Applicants must establish the experience required for the license classification they are pursuing. Experience documentation must satisfy the Board’s rules and application instructions. Complete the examination application. Candidates may use the application process provided by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Plumbing, Heating, and Fire Sprinkler Contractors. Submit supporting information. Required employment statements, experience records, identity information, background documentation, fees, and other materials must be submitted as directed by the Board. Receive examination approval. The Board reviews the application and determines whether the applicant has met the qualifications necessary to take the examination. Prepare and organize the approved books. Study the codes, review the Board’s testing rules, and prepare the books only in ways permitted by the examination-material policy. Complete the required examination. Follow the scheduling, identification, security, reference-material, and testing-site instructions issued for the approved examination. Complete the licensing process. Passing the examination is one component of licensure. The applicant must complete any remaining Board requirements before a license is issued or activated. State Requirements The North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Plumbing, Heating, and Fire Sprinkler Contractors establishes the qualifications for fuel piping contractor licensure. Its responsibilities include reviewing applications, determining examination eligibility, issuing licenses, enforcing Board laws and rules, investigating complaints, and regulating licensed work. Applicants must meet the experience and qualification standards applicable to the license sought. The Board requires documented on-site experience related to the installation, maintenance, service, or repair of systems within the category for which the applicant is seeking licensure. The amount and type of experience required depend on the specific contractor or technician classification. Applicants pursuing contractor licensure should use the contractor application rather than an application intended for a technician or another license category. North Carolina distinguishes between contractor and technician credentials, and the scope, experience requirements, and responsibilities may differ. The application must include accurate information about the applicant, employment history, qualifying experience, and any other matters requested by the Board. Supporting statements may need to be completed by licensed employers or other individuals qualified to verify the applicant’s work experience. Fuel piping contractors are responsible for complying with the laws and rules governing their licenses. These responsibilities may include proper supervision, adherence to the permitted scope of work, compliance with state construction codes, observance of inspection and permitting requirements, and professional conduct when contracting with customers. Licensure is not based solely on examination performance. The Board evaluates the complete application and supporting documentation. Applicants should ensure that all forms are complete, signatures are provided where required, and requested records are submitted in the proper format. Reference Books North Carolina Administration Code and Policies, 2018 EditionThis reference addresses the administration and enforcement of North Carolina construction-code requirements. It supports study of permits, inspections, approvals, responsibilities, code interpretations, administrative procedures, and statewide policies affecting regulated construction work. North Carolina Fuel Gas Code, 2018 EditionThe primary technical reference for fuel-gas systems. It covers piping materials, system sizing, installation, regulators, valves, appliance connections, pressure testing, combustion air, venting, equipment requirements, and safety provisions for fuel-gas work. North Carolina Mechanical Code, 2018 EditionThis code addresses mechanical systems and equipment, including installation requirements, ventilation, exhaust, combustion-related systems, clearances, ducts, equipment locations, and other mechanical provisions that may interact with fuel piping work. North Carolina Residential Code, 2018 EditionThis reference contains construction requirements applicable to one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses within the code’s scope. It includes residential mechanical and fuel-gas provisions relevant to piping, appliances, combustion air, venting, and installation practices. NC Board's Laws & Rules – 2026 EditionThis current Board publication contains the statutes and administrative rules governing North Carolina plumbing, heating, fuel piping, and fire sprinkler licensing. It supports study of license classifications, applications, examinations, supervision, contractor duties, prohibited practices, enforcement, and disciplinary authority. Test Information and Study Materials Effective exam preparation begins with a clear understanding of how the references work together. Fuel piping systems do not exist independently from appliances, mechanical systems, residential construction requirements, inspections, and contractor regulations. Study each book individually, then practice applying multiple references to the same project scenario. Start with definitions. Code questions often depend on the precise meaning of words such as appliance, approved, regulator, vent, connector, piping system, dwelling, permit, inspection, contractor, and responsible supervision. A common mistake is answering according to everyday usage rather than the code definition. Next, study the organization of the Fuel Gas Code. Become familiar with general regulations, piping-system design, pipe sizing, materials, installation, inspection, testing, appliances, combustion air, and venting. Learn how tables, footnotes, exceptions, and referenced sections affect the main rule. Use the Mechanical Code to review equipment-related requirements that may overlap with fuel piping work. Pay attention to appliance and equipment locations, ventilation, exhaust, access, protection, clearances, and installation standards. Review the Residential Code for similar subjects within residential construction. Administrative questions require a different study approach. Create a map of where to find permit rules, inspection responsibilities, approvals, code enforcement procedures, and Board licensing requirements. The Administrative Code and Policies book and the Board’s Laws & Rules publication should be treated as separate resources with different functions. Practice reading full sections rather than stopping at the first sentence that appears to answer a question. Many code provisions include exceptions, limitations, conditions, or references to other sections. Read the section heading, main text, exceptions, tables, footnotes, and cross-references before selecting an answer. Build speed by completing mixed-topic practice. Answer several questions involving pipe sizing, then move to testing, appliance installation, residential requirements, permits, inspections, and licensing rules. Mixed practice strengthens the ability to identify the correct book under time pressure. On examination day, read the question carefully and identify the central issue before opening a reference. Convert the issue into likely index terms. Eliminate answer choices that clearly conflict with the code, and use the book to confirm the remaining choice. When a question takes too long, mark it according to the testing system’s available process and return after completing more manageable items. How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal 1 Exam Prep helps candidates approach the North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor examination with a more organized study structure. This package assembles the listed code and licensing references so candidates can concentrate on learning the material and developing efficient open-book navigation skills. Organized study guidance helps divide a broad examination into manageable areas. Candidates can focus separately on fuel-gas piping, mechanical systems, residential work, code administration, and Board requirements before combining those topics in mixed review sessions. Trade-focused preparation encourages practical understanding rather than isolated memorization. Fuel piping questions may involve sizing, system pressure, approved materials, valves, regulators, testing procedures, appliance connections, combustion air, venting, protection from damage, or equipment location. Reviewing these subjects as parts of a complete system can make code provisions easier to understand and apply. Reference navigation is also an important part of preparation. Candidates should know which book addresses a topic, where major chapters begin, how the index describes technical terms, and how to follow cross-references. Practice-oriented preparation helps turn the books into working tools rather than unfamiliar materials carried into the examination room. 1 Exam Prep also supports confidence-building through consistent study habits. A structured schedule, repeated code searches, topic review, and timed practice can help candidates become more comfortable with the examination format. No course or book package can guarantee an exam result, but focused preparation can help candidates enter the test with a clearer plan and stronger familiarity with their references. Frequently Asked Questions What books are included in the North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor Exam Book Package? The package includes the North Carolina Administration Code and Policies, 2018 Edition; North Carolina Fuel Gas Code, 2018 Edition; North Carolina Mechanical Code, 2018 Edition; North Carolina Residential Code, 2018 Edition; and the NC Board's Laws & Rules, 2026 Edition. Is the North Carolina Fuel Piping Contractor exam open book? Yes. Candidates are expected to bring the approved references required for their examination. All books must comply with the Board’s current examination-material rules. What topics should I study for the fuel piping examination? Preparation should include fuel-gas piping materials, sizing, installation, pressure testing, valves, regulators, appliance connections, combustion air, venting, mechanical requirements, residential provisions, permits, inspections, code administration, and Board licensing rules. Which book is the main technical reference for fuel piping? The North Carolina Fuel Gas Code is the primary technical reference for fuel-gas piping systems, appliances, combustion air, venting, testing, and related installation requirements. Why are the Mechanical Code and Residential Code included? Fuel piping work often interacts with mechanical equipment, ventilation, appliance installation, combustion air, venting, and residential construction requirements. These codes help candidates address those connected subjects. What does the Board’s Laws & Rules book cover? The Board’s Laws & Rules publication addresses licensing classifications, examination requirements, contractor responsibilities, supervision, applications, prohibited conduct, enforcement, and disciplinary provisions. Can I write notes inside the books before the exam? The Board restricts alterations and additions to examination references. Candidates should follow the current published rules regarding highlighting, tabs, handwritten notes, inserts, and other book preparation. Do I need work experience before applying? Yes. Applicants must satisfy the experience requirements established for the license classification they are pursuing and provide acceptable documentation through the Board’s application process. Does passing the exam automatically create a contractor license? No. Passing the examination is one part of the licensing process. The Board must approve the applicant’s qualifications, experience, documentation, and remaining licensing requirements before issuing or activating a license. How should I prepare for an open-book code exam? Learn the concepts, study the organization of every book, review indexes and definitions, practice locating code sections, read exceptions and cross-references, and complete timed mixed-topic exercises. Can this package guarantee that I will pass the examination? No. Examination results depend on the candidate’s preparation, experience, understanding of the codes, familiarity with the references, and performance during the test.

Understand how walls, ceilings, floors, windows, doors, infiltration, ventilation, occupancy, internal gains, and outdoor design conditions influence the calculated load. Keep units organized and follow the method required by the applicable manual. For Manual D and Manual Q, study airflow, available static pressure, total effective length, friction rate, velocity, fitting losses, duct dimensions, branch layouts, and balancing. Practice mixed-reference questions as the examination approaches. Candidates learn to identify the correct reference, use indexes and tables effectively, follow calculation procedures, recognize exceptions, and confirm technical answers without relying on random searches. Reference-navigation practice is especially valuable for an examination with multiple code books and design manuals. Understanding the function of each publication can help candidates move directly to the most likely source and preserve testing time for calculations and more complex questions. 1 Exam Prep also promotes a confidence-building study structure based on repetition and realistic practice. The applicable Business and Law examination is a separate portion. How much experience is required? Heating Group 1 Class I Contractor applicants must document 4,000 hours of qualifying experience in the installation, maintenance, service, or repair of applicable heating systems. What is the difference between Class I and Class II? Class I applies to authorized work in commercial, residential, industrial, and institutional buildings. No. Applicants must also satisfy the experience, application, documentation, background-report, business-examination, and Board-approval requirements. Does the package guarantee a passing score? No. Results depend on the candidate’s experience, preparation, code knowledge, calculation skills, reference familiarity, and performance during the examination.

The individual or business must receive the applicable active license and comply with the Board’s requirements before performing work that requires licensure. description: North Carolina Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating Contractor (SP-PH) Exam Highlighted & Tabbed Book Package Prepare for the North Carolina Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating Contractor examination with a highlighted and tabbed book package covering electrical wiring for plumbing, heating, and air conditioning equipment, motors, compressors, pumps, controllers, branch circuits, feeders, conductors, disconnecting means, grounding, bonding, overcurrent protection, contractor licensing law, Board rules, business practices, and project management. The Special Restricted Plumbing, Heating, and Air Conditioning classification, commonly identified as SP-PH, is intended for professionals who perform qualifying electrical work as an incident to a lawful plumbing, heating, or air conditioning business. This restricted classification does not authorize general electrical contracting or electrical installations unrelated to the equipment served. This package includes the 2020 National Electrical Code as the approved examination-room reference. The NEC supports preparation involving HVAC and plumbing equipment, motors, compressors, pumps, controllers, branch circuits, feeders, disconnects, conductor sizing, grounding, bonding, raceways, boxes, overcurrent protection, control wiring, and electrical equipment installed in wet, damp, outdoor, or mechanical locations. The package also includes three closed-book study references that are not allowed in the examination room: Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, the Board’s Rules for the Implementation of the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, and the NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical Edition. All included trade books are highlighted and tabbed to support organized preparation and faster reference navigation. Permanent tabs help candidates locate major NEC articles, motor and compressor provisions, grounding requirements, licensing topics, Board rules, and contractor business subjects. Highlighting draws attention to important definitions, tables, calculations, limitations, exceptions, application procedures, and professional responsibilities. A highlighted and tabbed package can reduce the time spent searching through unfamiliar books and help candidates focus on understanding how the requirements apply. The markings are study aids, but candidates should still read complete sections, follow cross-references, review exceptions, and practice locating information under timed conditions. Plumbing, heating, and air conditioning systems may contain motors, compressors, pumps, air handlers, furnaces, boilers, heat pumps, condensing units, package units, refrigeration equipment, control transformers, thermostats, relays, contactors, disconnecting means, and related electrical components. Candidates should understand how general NEC requirements apply to these components and how the SP-PH scope limits the work that may be performed. The North Carolina Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating Contractor examination is open book, but only the approved 2020 National Electrical Code may be used in the examination room for this classification. The licensing law, Board rules, and NASCLA business reference are included for closed-book study and cannot be consulted during the test. Please allow an additional 15 business days for highlighted and tabbed trade book package orders. This additional processing period allows the books to be organized, highlighted, and tabbed before shipment. What You Get Highlighted and Tabbed Book: National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 Highlighted and Tabbed Study Book: Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, General Statutes Chapter 87, Article 4 Highlighted and Tabbed Study Book: The Board’s Rules for the Implementation of the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, Title 21, North Carolina Administrative Code, Chapter 18B Highlighted and Tabbed Study Book: NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical Edition Technical Preparation: Organized study support for motors, compressors, pumps, controllers, conductors, branch circuits, feeders, disconnecting means, grounding, bonding, and overcurrent protection. Licensing Preparation: Study support for North Carolina electrical contractor law, Board rules, applicant qualifications, restricted scope, and listed qualified individual responsibilities. Business Preparation: Review material covering contracts, estimating, financial management, project administration, safety, employment practices, insurance, and risk management. Processing: Please allow an additional 15 business days for highlighted and tabbed trade book package orders. Exam Details The North Carolina Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating Contractor examination contains 40 multiple-choice questions. Candidates have a maximum of three hours to complete the examination. The examination is administered after the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors approves the applicant. Candidates must receive examination authorization before scheduling a testing appointment. The SP-PH examination evaluates technical, legal, and business knowledge associated with electrical work for plumbing, heating, and air conditioning equipment. Candidates should prepare for questions involving motors, compressors, pumps, controllers, branch circuits, feeders, conductors, overload protection, short-circuit and ground-fault protection, grounding, bonding, disconnecting means, raceways, boxes, licensing law, Board rules, and contractor business practices. Motor questions may involve full-load current, conductor sizing, overload protection, branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection, feeder sizing, controller ratings, disconnect ratings, and the use of NEC motor tables. Candidates should understand that conductor sizing, motor overload protection, and branch-circuit protection are separate calculations governed by different Code provisions. Air conditioning and refrigeration questions may involve hermetic refrigerant motor-compressors, multimotor equipment, nameplate ratings, minimum circuit ampacity, maximum overcurrent protection, disconnecting means, equipment grounding, and branch-circuit conductor requirements. Equipment preparation may include furnaces, boilers, heat pumps, condensing units, air handlers, package units, pumps, fans, blowers, refrigeration equipment, circulation systems, water heaters, humidifiers, and related control systems. Feeder and branch-circuit preparation may include connected-load calculations, continuous loads, conductor ampacity, correction factors, adjustment factors, terminal temperature limitations, voltage drop, and overcurrent-device selection. Control-circuit questions may address control transformers, thermostats, relays, contactors, pressure switches, float switches, low-voltage controls, equipment interlocks, overcurrent protection, and wiring that extends beyond the immediate equipment location. Grounding and bonding preparation should include equipment grounding conductors, bonding of metal enclosures and raceways, effective ground-fault current paths, grounding electrode systems, grounding electrode conductors, and connections to plumbing, heating, and air conditioning equipment. Raceway and cable questions may address rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, electrical metallic tubing, PVC conduit, flexible metal conduit, liquidtight flexible conduit, cable assemblies, support, bends, fittings, physical protection, raceway fill, wet locations, and outdoor installations. Disconnecting-means preparation should include location, accessibility, visibility, ratings, markings, permitted device types, and the relationship among the disconnect, controller, motor, compressor, and overcurrent protective device. Business and law questions may involve license classifications, applications, experience qualifications, contracts, estimating, project scheduling, financial controls, employment practices, insurance, safety programs, permits, inspections, recordkeeping, license use, and the responsibilities of a listed qualified individual. Open Book Test The North Carolina Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating Contractor examination is an open-book test. The 2020 National Electrical Code is the only reference from this package allowed in the examination room for the SP-PH classification. The highlighted and tabbed NEC is organized to support navigation to major motor, compressor, branch-circuit, feeder, grounding, bonding, disconnect, raceway, conductor, and overcurrent-protection requirements. The Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, Board rules, and NASCLA business reference are included for closed-book preparation. Candidates should review these books thoroughly before the examination because licensing and business questions must be answered without consulting them during the test. The NEC may be brought in an approved softbound, spiral-bound, or hardbound format. Loose-leaf references and incomplete copies are not permitted. The reference may be highlighted, underlined, and annotated before the examination. Pencil notes must be highlighted, while notes written in pen do not need to be highlighted. Candidates may not write in the reference during the examination session. Permanent tabs may be used when they comply with current testing requirements. Temporary tabs, removable notes, divider tabs, loose sheets, attached papers, and unauthorized inserts are not allowed. Open-book testing requires familiarity with the NEC. Candidates should practice using the index, table of contents, definitions, article structure, tables, exceptions, and cross-references so they can locate information efficiently. A question involving an air conditioning unit may require the equipment nameplate provisions and the NEC article covering air conditioning and refrigeration equipment. A question involving a pump motor may require the general motor provisions and applicable motor tables. A conductor-sizing question may require the equipment nameplate, an ampacity table, terminal temperature limitations, and correction or adjustment factors. A grounding question may require both the general grounding article and requirements specific to the equipment or wiring method. Timed code-navigation practice can help candidates use the three-hour examination period effectively. A practical approach is to identify the subject, select the applicable NEC article, locate the correct section or table, and determine whether an exception or special condition applies. Licensing Steps Confirm the SP-PH classification. Review the restricted scope and determine whether it matches the plumbing, heating, or air conditioning electrical work the applicant intends to perform. Document qualifying experience. Collect records showing the required primary, secondary, or other recognized electrical and trade-field experience. Confirm the business relationship. The applicant must be primarily engaged in or regularly employed by a lawful plumbing, heating, or air conditioning business in North Carolina and prepared to serve as its listed qualified individual. Complete the examination application. Submit the required personal, employment, experience, and business information to the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Provide required supporting statements. Include character references, experience verification, and other documentation requested with the application. Submit the examination fee. Include the applicable payment with the completed application. Receive Board approval. The Board reviews the application and determines whether the applicant satisfies the examination qualifications. Receive examination authorization. Approved candidates receive instructions for scheduling the examination. Schedule the examination. Register with the testing provider and select an appointment within the authorized period. Prepare the 2020 NEC. Confirm that the highlighted and tabbed reference complies with current rules involving binding, notes, highlighting, and permanent tabs. Complete the examination. Bring the required identification and approved NEC reference to the testing center. Complete the licensing process. After passing, satisfy the remaining Board requirements for the individual or business entity seeking the SP-PH license. Maintain the license. Follow current renewal, continuing education, listed qualified individual, supervision, and compliance requirements. State Requirements The North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors regulates the SP-PH examination and license. The Board establishes applicant qualifications, reviews experience, authorizes examinations, issues licenses, and enforces the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law and related rules. An applicant for the Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating classification must document at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience. At least 2,000 hours must be primary experience. The remaining hours may consist of primary experience, secondary experience, or a combination of both. Applicants may receive credit for qualifying service gained in the plumbing, heating, or air conditioning field when the experience falls within categories recognized by the Board. Experience must be documented according to the examination application requirements. The applicant must verify that the applicant is primarily engaged in or regularly employed by a lawful plumbing, heating, or air conditioning business in North Carolina and will serve as the listed qualified individual for that business. The SP-PH license authorizes installation, maintenance, or repair of electrical wiring or devices only as an incident to the license holder’s plumbing, heating, or air conditioning business. The authorized wiring must be directly related to plumbing, heating, or air conditioning equipment. It is limited to circuits or portions of circuits operating at no more than 600 volts phase to phase. The equipment wiring must be electrically isolated from the building wiring system by an overcurrent protective device, such as a fused switch or circuit breaker, installed with complete line-side connections by others. The protective device must be permanently and legibly marked to identify the equipment it serves. It may be located in an enclosure intended solely for the specific equipment or in a building panelboard when the required downstream wiring and disconnecting arrangement have been installed by others. When the protective device is located in a building panelboard, wiring must be installed by others from the load-side terminals to a junction box, auxiliary gutter, or similar disconnecting point outside the panelboard. That point must be located in sight of and within 50 feet of the equipment served. The electrical work authorized by the SP-PH classification begins at the load-side terminals of the protective isolating device. Line-side building wiring is outside the restricted scope. Except for qualifying control wiring, the authorized wiring must remain physically adjacent to the plumbing, heating, or air conditioning equipment. Control wiring receiving power from the equipment may extend beyond that area when the control voltage does not exceed 120 volts to ground and the wiring is protected from overcurrent. Wiring performed under the SP-PH classification may not be installed in a location classified as hazardous under the National Electrical Code. The SP-PH license does not authorize general electrical contracting or unrelated electrical installations. All work must remain within the scope established for plumbing, heating, and air conditioning equipment. Special restricted classifications are not subject to the same project-value limits that apply to regular Limited and Intermediate electrical contractor licenses. The absence of a project-value limit does not expand the type of work authorized. Passing the examination does not independently authorize electrical contracting. The appropriate license must be issued and active before the individual or business performs or offers to perform work requiring the SP-PH classification. Reference Books National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020This highlighted and tabbed examination-room reference covers motors, compressors, pumps, controllers, branch circuits, feeders, conductors, raceways, boxes, grounding, bonding, disconnecting means, overload protection, and short-circuit and ground-fault protection. Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, General Statutes Chapter 87, Article 4This highlighted and tabbed closed-book study reference addresses Board authority, electrical contractor licensing, classifications, examinations, qualified individuals, violations, enforcement, and statutory responsibilities. It is not allowed in the examination room. The Board’s Rules for the Implementation of the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, Title 21, North Carolina Administrative Code, Chapter 18BThis highlighted and tabbed closed-book study reference covers experience requirements, examination procedures, license classifications, SP-PH scope, renewals, continuing education, violations, and listed qualified individual responsibilities. It is not allowed in the examination room. NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical EditionThis highlighted and tabbed closed-book study reference supports preparation involving business organization, contracts, estimating, financial management, project administration, employment practices, safety, insurance, recordkeeping, and risk management. It is not allowed in the examination room. Exam Room Approved Books National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020This highlighted and tabbed reference is the only book from the package allowed in the examination room for the North Carolina Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating Contractor examination. Test Information and Study Materials Build a study plan around motors, compressors, pumps, controllers, branch circuits, feeders, conductor ampacity, overload protection, short-circuit protection, grounding, bonding, disconnecting means, raceways, HVAC equipment, licensing law, Board rules, and contractor business practices. Use the highlighted and tabbed 2020 NEC to review motor full-load current, compressor requirements, equipment nameplates, minimum circuit ampacity, maximum overcurrent protection, conductor sizing, controller ratings, disconnect ratings, and grounding requirements. Practice distinguishing between motor overload protection and branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection. These devices perform different functions and are selected under different NEC rules. Review wiring methods for outdoor, damp, wet, mechanical, and equipment locations. Pay attention to flexible connections, conductor insulation, physical protection, support, fittings, grounding, bonding, and enclosure ratings. Use timed reference-navigation exercises. Read the question, identify the electrical subject, locate the applicable NEC article or table, review the complete requirement, and determine whether an exception, definition, nameplate provision, or cross-reference applies. Study the licensing law and Board rules separately because they are not available during the examination. Focus on the SP-PH scope, qualifying experience, application requirements, listed qualified individual responsibilities, renewals, continuing education, and prohibited conduct. Review the NASCLA business reference for contracts, estimating, scheduling, financial controls, employment responsibilities, insurance, safety administration, project documentation, and risk management. How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal 1 Exam Prep helps North Carolina Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating Contractor candidates organize technical, licensing, and business references into a practical preparation structure. Highlighted and tabbed books support faster access to major NEC articles, motor and compressor provisions, licensing sections, Board rules, and business topics. This organization helps candidates spend more time understanding the material and less time searching through unfamiliar pages. Trade-focused review connects National Electrical Code requirements with plumbing, heating, and air conditioning equipment, including motors, compressors, pumps, controllers, conductors, disconnects, grounding, bonding, overload protection, and overcurrent protection. Practice-oriented preparation helps candidates identify the subject of a question, locate the applicable NEC article or table, review the governing requirement, and apply the information efficiently. Reference-navigation practice builds familiarity with the 2020 NEC index, definitions, articles, tables, exceptions, and cross-references. These skills support more effective use of the approved book during the three-hour open-book examination. Closed-book study guidance helps candidates review the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, Board rules, restricted SP-PH scope, experience qualifications, and business-management subjects that cannot be referenced during the test. Confidence-building study structure helps candidates divide a broad examination into manageable technical, regulatory, and business sections while maintaining consistent preparation. No book package can guarantee examination passage or license issuance. Results depend on the candidate’s experience, qualifications, preparation, familiarity with the NEC, understanding of plumbing and HVAC electrical systems, and performance during the examination. Frequently Asked Questions What books are included in this package? The package includes the highlighted and tabbed 2020 National Electrical Code, Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, the Board’s electrical contracting rules, and the NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical Edition. Are the books highlighted and tabbed? Yes. The included trade references are highlighted and tabbed to support organized preparation and faster navigation. How long does processing take? Please allow an additional 15 business days for highlighted and tabbed trade book package orders. Is the SP-PH examination open book? Yes. The examination is open book, but only the approved 2020 National Electrical Code may be used in the examination room. Are the licensing law, Board rules, and NASCLA book allowed in the examination room? No. Those references are included for closed-book study and are not allowed in the testing room. How many questions are on the examination? The North Carolina Special Restricted Plumbing and Heating Contractor examination contains 40 multiple-choice questions. How much time is allowed? Candidates have a maximum of three hours to complete the examination. How much experience is required? Applicants must document at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 2,000 hours of primary experience. What work does the SP-PH license authorize? The license authorizes electrical wiring and devices directly related to plumbing, heating, or air conditioning equipment as an incident to the license holder’s lawful trade business. Where does the authorized wiring begin? The authorized wiring begins at the load-side terminals of the overcurrent protective isolating device installed and connected on the line side by others. What is the maximum voltage permitted under the SP-PH scope? The authorized wiring is limited to circuits or portions of circuits operating at no more than 600 volts phase to phase. Can control wiring extend beyond the immediate equipment area? Qualifying control wiring may extend beyond the immediate equipment area when it receives control power from the equipment, does not exceed 120 volts to ground, and is protected from overcurrent. Can SP-PH wiring be installed in hazardous locations? No. Wiring performed under the SP-PH classification may not be installed in a location classified as hazardous under the National Electrical Code. Does the SP-PH license authorize general electrical contracting? No. The license is limited to qualifying electrical work directly related to plumbing, heating, and air conditioning equipment. Can additional notes or tabs be added to the NEC? Only markings and permanent tabs permitted under current examination rules should be added. Temporary tabs, loose pages, removable notes, and unauthorized materials are not allowed. Does passing the examination automatically issue the license? No. Passing satisfies the examination requirement, but the applicant must complete the Board’s licensing process before performing work under the SP-PH classification.

The Single Family Detached Residential Dwelling classification, commonly identified as SP-SFD, is designed for electrical contractors who install, maintain, or repair wiring and electrical devices in or on qualifying single-family detached residential dwellings and their ancillary structures. The classification provides a defined residential scope and does not authorize unrestricted electrical contracting on commercial, industrial, multifamily, or attached residential properties. This package includes the 2020 National Electrical Code and NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, 2019 Edition. These technical references support preparation involving dwelling-unit services, feeders, branch circuits, receptacles, lighting outlets, appliances, grounding, bonding, smoke alarms, carbon monoxide detection interfaces, signaling equipment, fire alarm circuits, and residential electrical safety. The package also includes three closed-book study references that are not allowed in the examination room: Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, the Board’s Rules for the Implementation of the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, and the NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical Edition. These additional references support preparation involving North Carolina electrical contractor licensing, applicant qualifications, license classifications, project limitations, qualified-individual responsibilities, contracts, estimating, financial management, employment practices, safety, insurance, recordkeeping, project administration, and contractor compliance. Residential electrical work involves much more than installing receptacles and lighting. Candidates should understand service equipment, panelboards, grounding electrode systems, branch-circuit calculations, required outlets, appliance circuits, arc-fault protection, ground-fault protection, conductor sizing, box fill, cable installation, smoke alarms, lighting controls, outdoor wiring, garages, accessory structures, and equipment serving the dwelling. The North Carolina SP-SFD examination is open book. The 2020 NEC and NFPA 72, 2019 Edition, are the technical exam-room references included in this package. The licensing law, Board rules, and NASCLA business reference are included for closed-book preparation and cannot be consulted during the examination. This package provides a practical group of technical, licensing, and business references for candidates preparing to demonstrate their knowledge of single-family residential electrical contracting. It supports organized review of dwelling wiring requirements while reinforcing the legal scope and professional responsibilities associated with the North Carolina SP-SFD license. Exam Details The North Carolina Special Restricted Single Family Detached Residential Dwelling Contractor examination contains 40 multiple-choice questions. Service and feeder preparation may include load calculations, service ratings, service conductors, service disconnects, grounding electrode conductors, neutral conductors, panelboards, feeder sizing, dwelling-unit demand factors, and equipment grounding requirements. Branch-circuit questions may involve required small-appliance circuits, laundry circuits, bathroom circuits, garage receptacles, outdoor outlets, kitchen receptacles, lighting outlets, appliance circuits, conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, and multiwire branch circuits. Dwelling-unit receptacle preparation should include spacing requirements, wall-space measurements, countertop and work-surface outlets, kitchen islands and peninsulas, bathroom receptacles, garages, basements, hallways, foyers, outdoor locations, balconies, decks, and accessory buildings. Ground-fault circuit-interrupter preparation may involve kitchens, bathrooms, garages, basements, crawl spaces, laundry areas, outdoor locations, sinks, dishwashers, and other dwelling-unit areas where GFCI protection is required. Arc-fault circuit-interrupter preparation may address the dwelling areas and branch circuits requiring AFCI protection, permitted protection methods, circuit extensions, replacement devices, and coordination with other protective requirements. Fire alarm and smoke alarm preparation may involve alarm placement, interconnection, power supplies, secondary power, notification, testing, inspection, replacement, and the relationship between residential alarms and fire alarm system requirements. Include written statements from at least two people attesting to the applicant’s good character. Submit experience verification. Provide the records and statements needed to document qualifying electrical experience. Submit the required examination fee. Include the applicable payment with the completed application. Bring the required identification and approved technical references to the testing center. Review the score report. Examination results are provided after the test is completed. The Board establishes applicant qualifications, reviews experience, authorizes examinations, issues licenses, and enforces the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law and Board rules. An applicant for the Single Family Detached Residential Dwelling classification must be at least 18 years of age and document at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience. At least 2,000 hours must be primary experience. The remaining hours may consist of primary experience, secondary experience, or a combination of both. Primary experience generally includes direct involvement in the installation of electrical wiring and equipment governed by the NEC or work activities directly related to those installations. Secondary experience may include recognized electrical training or related work performed in a supporting capacity. The SP-SFD license authorizes the installation, maintenance, or repair of electrical wiring and devices in or on a qualifying single-family residential dwelling or in structures ancillary to that dwelling. A single-family residential dwelling is a building or manufactured home designed and used for habitation by one family and not physically attached to another building or structure. Cabanas, porches, room additions, and qualifying ancillary structures may be treated as part of the dwelling when designed and used for residential purposes by its occupants. Ancillary structures may include a detached residential garage or carport, household or farm equipment storage shed, barn, pump house, electric fence, or yard lighting associated with the dwelling. Passing the SP-SFD examination does not independently authorize electrical contracting. The applicable license must be issued and active before the individual or business offers to perform or performs work requiring the classification. The markings are study aids, but candidates should still read complete sections, follow cross-references, review exceptions, and practice locating information under timed conditions. Exam Details The North Carolina Special Restricted Swimming Pool Bonding Contractor examination contains 25 multiple-choice questions. Swimming pool bonding preparation should include the purpose of equipotential bonding and the difference between bonding and grounding. Bonding connects conductive parts together to reduce voltage gradients, while grounding connects electrical systems and equipment to the grounding system under applicable NEC requirements.
