title: 2023 North Carolina Master Electrician Exam Prep Study Package Includes Instructor Led NEC Course (Based on the 2023 NEC)
description: 2023 North Carolina Master Electrician Exam Prep Study Package Includes Instructor-Led NEC Course (Based on the 2023 NEC) Prepare for advanced North Carolina electrical contractor licensing with a comprehensive study package built around the 2023 National Electrical Code. This North Carolina Master Electrician Exam Prep Study Package combines the NFPA 70 National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition, NEC tabs, master electrician flash cards, a Master Electrician Study Guide, a Calculations Study Guide, an online instructor-led NEC course, simulated practice exams, an NEC overview, and live and recorded instructional videos. North Carolina does not use a statewide electrical license formally titled Master Electrician. Instead, the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors licenses electrical contractors in Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited classifications. The Unlimited classification represents the highest regular electrical contracting classification and allows the licensee to engage in electrical contracting projects without a project-value limitation. Preparing for a North Carolina electrical contracting examination requires more than practical field experience. Candidates must understand electrical theory, National Electrical Code requirements, electrical calculations, plan interpretation, estimating principles, fire alarm requirements, and North Carolina electrical contracting laws and rules. Candidates must also learn how to locate technical information efficiently while working within a six-hour examination period. This study package provides an organized way to develop those skills. Instead of relying on one book or a single type of exam preparation, students can read focused study materials, complete electrical calculations, review important concepts with flash cards, follow instructor-led lessons, practice NEC navigation, and measure their progress through simulated practice exams. The included NFPA 70 National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition, serves as the foundation of the online NEC course. The included NEC tabs help organize major chapters, articles, definitions, and tables so students can practice locating information efficiently. Repeated navigation work helps electricians understand how general requirements, specialized rules, tables, exceptions, and related articles connect to one another. The Master Electrician Study Guide provides a structured path through advanced electrical topics. The Calculations Study Guide supports focused practice with electrical theory, conductor sizing, branch circuits, feeders, services, motors, transformers, load calculations, raceway fill, box fill, voltage drop, and other mathematical subjects associated with professional electrical work. Master electrician flash cards provide convenient review for formulas, terminology, definitions, electrical relationships, and code concepts. The online course adds live instructor-led training, recorded lessons, a guided NEC overview, and simulated practice exams that can be completed around work, business, and family responsibilities. This package and course are based on the 2023 NEC. The current North Carolina electrical contractor examination handbook identifies the 2020 National Electrical Code as the required examination-room reference. Candidates should prepare with the exact 2020 NEC required for the official North Carolina examination while using this package to strengthen broader NEC knowledge, calculations, and master-level electrical skills. What You Get NFPA 70 National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition: The primary electrical code book used throughout the included instructor-led NEC course. NEC Tabs: Tabs designed to organize major NEC articles and support faster navigation during study sessions. Master Electrician Flash Cards: Portable review tools for reinforcing electrical terminology, formulas, definitions, and code concepts. Master Electrician Study Guide: A structured preparation resource covering advanced electrical knowledge and contractor-level exam topics. Calculations Study Guide: Focused material for electrical mathematics, loads, conductor sizing, motors, transformers, voltage drop, raceway fill, box fill, and related problems. Online Instructor-Led NEC Course: Guided electrical code instruction based on the 2023 National Electrical Code. Simulated Practice Exams: Exam-style questions designed to help students apply electrical knowledge, practice pacing, and identify weak subjects. NEC Overview: Instruction covering the organization, structure, and practical use of the National Electrical Code. Live Videos: Instructor-led sessions providing organized guidance through important electrical concepts and calculations. Recorded Videos: Flexible lessons that can be paused and replayed while reviewing difficult subjects. Exam Details The North Carolina Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited Electrical Contractor examinations are administered by PSI for the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Candidates must apply to the Board and receive approval before registering for the examination. Each of the three regular electrical contractor examinations contains 100 multiple-choice questions. Candidates receive a maximum of six hours to complete the examination. The examinations are developed by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. They evaluate the technical and practical knowledge needed to perform and supervise electrical contracting work safely and in accordance with North Carolina requirements. Examination subjects include National Electrical Code requirements, analysis of electrical plans and specifications, electrical calculations, estimating, fundamentals of electrical installation, fire alarm requirements, North Carolina electrical contracting laws, Board rules, and business-related subjects applicable to electrical contractors. NEC preparation should include branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding and bonding, conductors, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, raceways, boxes, equipment, motors, transformers, special occupancies, special equipment, emergency systems, and related electrical installations. Electrical calculation preparation is also important. Candidates should practice service and feeder loads, conductor sizing, motor circuits, transformer calculations, voltage drop, raceway fill, box fill, grounding conductors, demand factors, and other mathematical subjects encountered in electrical contracting. The examination also includes plan-reading work. Candidates should become comfortable identifying electrical symbols, interpreting lighting and power plans, determining circuit and equipment requirements, and connecting information shown on drawings with applicable electrical code provisions. Questions concerning North Carolina electrical contracting law, Board rules, and the North Carolina electrical edition of the NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management are included in the examination. These questions are treated differently from the open-book electrical-code portion because candidates cannot consult those documents during the test. The simulated practice exams included with this package help students work through technical questions in an exam-oriented format. Practice testing can identify weaknesses in calculations, NEC navigation, electrical theory, plan reading, trade knowledge, or time management before the official examination. Open Book Test The North Carolina Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited Electrical Contractor examinations are open-book tests for the approved electrical references. Candidates are required to bring their own approved reference books to the PSI examination center. The current examination handbook requires the 2020 National Electrical Code. Candidates taking the Limited, Intermediate, or Unlimited examination must also bring the 2013 edition of NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code. The 2023 NEC included with this study package is used for course instruction and exam preparation. Candidates should also obtain the 2020 NEC required for their official North Carolina examination and practice with that edition before test day. Approved references may be highlighted, underlined, and annotated before the examination. Notes written directly on the pages are allowed when prepared according to the Board’s testing rules. Candidates may not write in the reference books during the examination session. Permanent tabs are permitted. Temporary tabs such as Post-It notes, stapled tabs, and divider tabs are not allowed. The NEC tabs included with this package can support study navigation, and candidates should make sure any tabs used in the official examination reference meet the Board’s permanent-tab requirements. Loose papers and additional attached papers are prohibited inside the examination references. References must be complete and properly bound. The testing center provides calculators, scratch paper, and pencils. Although the examination is open book for the approved electrical references, questions based on North Carolina electrical contracting law, Board rules, and the NASCLA business and project-management reference are closed book. Candidates must prepare those subjects before the examination rather than depending on reference lookup during the test. An open-book exam still requires extensive preparation. With 100 questions and a six-hour time limit, candidates need to recognize the subject of a question quickly, identify the likely NEC article or table, and locate the controlling provision without unnecessary searching. Licensing Steps Begin by selecting the North Carolina electrical contracting classification that matches your experience and contracting goals. The regular classifications are Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited. The Limited examination requires at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience. At least 2,000 hours must be primary electrical experience involving direct work with electrical wiring and equipment governed by the National Electrical Code. The Intermediate examination requires at least 5,750 hours of qualifying experience. At least 5,000 hours must be primary electrical experience. The Unlimited examination requires at least 9,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 8,000 hours of primary experience. Unlimited applicants must also submit statements from at least two people knowledgeable about the applicant’s electrical experience and ability to supervise and direct electrical contracting work at the Unlimited level. Complete the Board’s examination application for the classification being pursued. Applicants must be at least 18 years old and submit the required experience and character documentation. The Board reviews the examination application and determines whether the candidate satisfies the eligibility requirements. Approved candidates receive a Notice of Approval and an examination authorization period. PSI then provides registration instructions. The examination must be scheduled and completed during the approved authorization period. An authorization includes one examination attempt. Use the study package to create an organized preparation schedule. Begin with the NEC overview, work through the Master Electrician Study Guide, complete the Calculations Study Guide, and review the flash cards regularly. Attend live instructor-led lessons and use recorded videos to revisit difficult subjects. Complete simulated practice exams under realistic time limits and review every incorrect answer before attempting another practice exam. Before test day, prepare the approved 2020 NEC and 2013 NFPA 72 reference materials according to the current examination rules. Review North Carolina laws, Board rules, business subjects, and the lighting and power plans included with the official examination materials. After passing the examination, complete the New License Application to obtain and activate the electrical contracting license. Passing the examination qualifies the individual for the applicable classification, but the licensing process must still be completed before engaging in electrical contracting under the new credential. State Requirements Electrical contracting in North Carolina is regulated by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. A person, partnership, firm, or corporation engaged in electrical contracting must hold the appropriate Board-issued license unless a specific statutory exemption applies. The Limited classification allows electrical contracting projects within the project-value and voltage limitations established by North Carolina law and Board rules. The current rule-based project-value limit is $60,000 for a single project. The Intermediate classification allows electrical contracting projects with a current rule-based single-project value limit of $150,000. The Unlimited classification allows the licensee to engage in electrical contracting projects regardless of project value. For electricians seeking the broadest regular North Carolina electrical contractor classification, Unlimited is the highest level. Each electrical contracting business must have at least one listed qualified individual at each separate place of business. The listed qualified individual has the specific duty and authority to supervise and direct electrical contracting performed under the license. Intermediate and Unlimited license applicants must also satisfy the Board’s financial qualification requirements by providing the required bonding-ability statement, line-of-credit documentation, or other accepted financial information. North Carolina also participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program. Candidates who have passed the qualifying NASCLA Electrical Contractor or Master Electrician examination may be eligible to pursue North Carolina Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, or certain special classifications through the Board’s NASCLA process. Qualified individuals listed on Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, and Single-Family Detached licenses must complete the Board-required continuing education for license renewal. Current rules require eight hours of approved continuing education for these classifications. Licensing does not replace electrical permitting, inspection, adopted code, or local administrative requirements. Electrical contractors remain responsible for performing work within the scope of their license and complying with applicable North Carolina electrical and building requirements. Reference Books NFPA 70 National Electrical Code, 2023 EditionThe primary electrical code book included with this package. description: North Carolina Special Restricted Elevator (SP-EL) Contractor Exam - Online Practice Questions Prepare for the North Carolina Special Restricted Elevator (SP-EL) Contractor examination with online practice questions designed around electrical code knowledge, elevator-related electrical systems, motors and controls, wiring methods, overcurrent protection, grounding, conductor sizing, North Carolina electrical licensing requirements, and contractor business knowledge. This online preparation helps candidates organize the material into manageable subjects while developing the reference-navigation skills needed for an open-book electrical contractor examination. The Special Restricted Elevator classification is regulated by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. SP-EL is a specialized electrical contracting license intended for businesses engaged in the elevator field. It does not provide unrestricted authority to perform general electrical contracting. Instead, it authorizes specific electrical work associated with elevators, dumbwaiters, escalators, moving walks, and personnel hoists. The primary exam-room reference for the SP-EL examination is the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020. Candidates should become comfortable using the NEC for conductor requirements, overcurrent protection, motors, controllers, disconnecting means, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, equipment requirements, and the specialized provisions applicable to elevators and related equipment. Additional preparation material includes the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, the Board's Rules for implementation of the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, and the NASCLA Contractors' Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical Edition. These materials are used for examination subject matter but are not permitted as candidate reference books inside the SP-EL testing room. Online practice questions can help candidates move beyond simply reading the NEC. By working through electrical calculations, code lookups, licensing questions, business concepts, and elevator-related electrical scenarios, candidates can identify which areas need additional review and build a more deliberate study plan. Exam Details The North Carolina Special Restricted Elevator (SP-EL) electrical contracting examination is administered through PSI for candidates approved by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Exam: North Carolina Special Restricted Elevator (SP-EL) Number of Questions: 40 multiple-choice questions Time Allowed: 3 hours Passing Score: 70% Testing Provider: PSI Primary Exam-Room Reference: National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 The SP-EL exam is one of North Carolina's Special Restricted electrical contracting examinations. Candidates should be prepared for questions involving general electrical principles as well as subjects that apply specifically to electrical installations associated with elevators and similar equipment. Motor and control wiring is an important area for SP-EL preparation. Candidates should understand branch-circuit and feeder ampacity, overload protection, short-circuit and ground-fault protection, disconnecting means, controllers, conductor sizing, and the relationship between motor loads and required electrical protection. Elevator-related electrical preparation should include the NEC provisions covering elevators, dumbwaiters, escalators, moving walks, platform lifts, and related equipment. Candidates should become familiar with wiring methods, traveling cables, equipment rooms and spaces, disconnecting means, lighting and receptacles, conductors, controls, and other electrical requirements that may apply within the authorized scope. General electrical knowledge is also important. Questions may require candidates to work with conductor ampacity, raceways, boxes and fittings, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, feeders, branch circuits, services, and other NEC topics that support safe installation and maintenance. Because the passing requirement is 70%, candidates should not focus exclusively on specialized elevator articles. Strong preparation should combine specialty knowledge with a working understanding of the broader NEC provisions used to solve electrical installation questions. Open Book Test The North Carolina SP-EL Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates are required to bring their own approved reference material to the PSI testing center. For the Special Restricted Elevator examination, the approved exam-room reference is: National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020 The NEC should be treated as a working examination tool rather than simply a book to bring on test day. Candidates should repeatedly practice using the index, articles, definitions, tables, notes, exceptions, and cross-references so they can locate information efficiently during the three-hour examination. Elevator-related questions may require candidates to navigate both specialty provisions and general electrical articles. For example, a question involving an elevator motor may require understanding both the specialized elevator requirements and general motor provisions. Other questions can combine conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, disconnect requirements, and equipment-specific conditions. The examination provider permits approved reference materials in bound form and establishes requirements concerning notes and tabs. Candidates should prepare their NEC in accordance with the current testing rules before arriving at the examination center. The following study materials are not allowed into the SP-EL examination room: Electrical Contractors Licensing Law - General Statutes Chapter 87, Article 4 The Board's Rules for the Implementation of the Electrical Contractors Licensing Law - Title 21, North Carolina Administrative Code, Chapter 18B NASCLA Contractors' Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical Edition Although these references are not permitted in the testing room, the examination includes subject matter drawn from electrical licensing law, Board rules, and contractor business knowledge. Candidates should therefore study these subjects thoroughly before testing rather than expecting to look up the answers during the examination. Licensing Steps The North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors administers the licensing process for Special Restricted Elevator contractors. Candidates should complete the applicable experience, examination, and license-activation requirements. Confirm the SP-EL classification. Determine that the Special Restricted Elevator license matches the electrical work performed as part of the elevator business. Meet the experience requirement. Applicants must establish the qualifying electrical and elevator-related experience required for the SP-EL classification. Confirm employment or business involvement in the elevator field. The applicant must provide information showing that the qualified individual is associated with a firm primarily engaged in the lawful elevator business. Prepare the examination application. Complete the required application and provide the experience information requested by the Board. Receive Board approval. The applicant must be approved before scheduling the examination. Receive PSI eligibility information. Approved candidates receive the information needed to create or use their PSI account and schedule testing. Prepare with the NEC 2020. Study general electrical requirements, motors, controls, feeders, branch circuits, grounding, wiring methods, and elevator-related provisions. Study North Carolina licensing law and Board rules. These materials are tested even though the books are not allowed into the examination room. Study contractor Business and Law. Review the North Carolina Electrical Edition of the NASCLA contractor business reference. Complete the SP-EL examination. Candidates have three hours to answer 40 multiple-choice questions and must achieve at least 70%. Apply for and activate the license. Passing the examination does not by itself activate an electrical contracting license. The applicable license application process must also be completed. State Requirements The Special Restricted Elevator classification is a limited electrical contracting license. It is intended for electrical work performed as an incident to a lawful elevator business rather than general electrical contracting. The SP-EL license authorizes the installation, maintenance, or repair of electrical wiring only when that wiring is an integral part of an elevator, dumbwaiter, escalator, moving walk, or personnel hoist. The authorized electrical wiring must be electrically isolated from the building wiring by a safety switch or circuit breaker installed with its line-side connections by others. SP-EL authority begins at the load-side terminals of that protective isolating device, commonly described as work beyond the disconnecting means. This distinction is important because the SP-EL license does not authorize a business to perform unrestricted building electrical work. Candidates should understand both what the classification permits and where its electrical authority begins and ends. Under the current examination handbook requirements, an SP-EL applicant must have at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience. At least 2,000 hours must be primary experience, while the remaining qualifying experience may be primary, secondary, or a combination of both. Creditable experience may also include qualifying work gained in the elevator field. The applicant must also provide information establishing that the applicant is primarily engaged in, or regularly employed by and intended to serve as the listed qualified individual for, a firm primarily engaged in a lawful elevator business in North Carolina. Special Restricted licenses are separate classifications designed for limited phases of electrical contracting. The SP-EL classification does not carry the general project-value limitations associated with North Carolina Limited or Intermediate regular electrical contracting licenses when the work remains within the authorized SP-EL scope. Qualified individuals listed on Special Restricted Elevator licenses are also subject to the continuing-education requirements established by the Board for renewal. Maintaining the license requires continued attention to applicable electrical code, licensing rules, and professional responsibilities after the initial examination is passed. Reference Books National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020This is the primary approved exam-room reference for the North Carolina SP-EL examination. It supports preparation involving motors, conductors, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, controllers, disconnecting means, elevator equipment, traveling cables, and other electrical requirements. Candidates should practice code navigation extensively before testing. Test Information and Study Materials A strong SP-EL preparation plan should combine electrical code navigation, elevator-specific electrical knowledge, calculations, North Carolina licensing rules, and contractor business preparation. Start with elevator-related NEC requirements. Become familiar with the provisions covering elevators, dumbwaiters, escalators, moving walks, and similar equipment. Study wiring methods, traveling cables, disconnecting means, equipment spaces, controls, and electrical installation requirements. Review motors and motor controls. Motor loads are particularly important for elevator-related electrical work. Practice branch-circuit sizing, feeder calculations, overload protection, short-circuit and ground-fault protection, disconnects, and controller requirements. Practice conductor calculations. Review conductor ampacity, adjustment and correction concepts, feeder sizing, branch-circuit sizing, and conductor requirements for motor loads. Calculation questions should be practiced until the required NEC tables and sections become familiar. Study grounding and bonding. Review equipment grounding conductors, grounding connections, bonding requirements, and the electrical safety principles that apply to elevator equipment and associated circuits. Review wiring methods. Study raceways, flexible wiring methods, boxes, fittings, conductor protection, permitted uses, and restrictions that can affect specialized equipment installations. Practice NEC navigation under time limits. Having three hours for 40 questions provides time for code lookups, but candidates should still avoid broad searches. Practice identifying the likely NEC article before opening the book. Study the books that cannot enter the exam. North Carolina Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, Board Rules, and NASCLA contractor business material must be learned during preparation. Candidates should understand the major concepts before test day because these references will not be available for lookup during the examination. Review missed practice questions. Determine whether each mistake came from an electrical calculation, code-navigation problem, misunderstanding of SP-EL scope, licensing-rule question, or contractor business concept. Then return to that specific subject for additional study. Understand the license scope. Questions about professional authority can be just as important as technical electrical questions. Know that SP-EL work is limited to electrical wiring integral to elevator-related equipment and begins beyond the required protective isolating device installed by others. SP-EL is the Special Restricted Elevator electrical contracting classification issued by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. How many questions are on the SP-EL examination? The Special Restricted Elevator examination contains 40 multiple-choice questions. How much time is allowed for the SP-EL exam? Candidates have a maximum of three hours to complete the examination. What score is required to pass? The passing score for the North Carolina electrical contractor examinations is 70%. Is the SP-EL exam open book? Yes. The Special Restricted Elevator examination is open book with the approved reference permitted in the PSI testing center. Which book can I take into the SP-EL examination? The approved exam-room reference for SP-EL is the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2020. Is NFPA 72 required for the SP-EL exam? No. NFPA 72 is required for certain other North Carolina electrical classifications, but it is not listed as an SP-EL exam-room reference. Which books are not allowed into the SP-EL exam? The Electrical Contractors Licensing Law, the Board's Rules for implementation of that law, and the NASCLA Contractors' Guide to Business, Law, and Project Management: North Carolina Electrical Edition are study materials and are not permitted as candidate reference books inside the SP-EL examination room. How much experience is required for the SP-EL examination? The current examination requirements call for at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 2,000 hours of primary experience. Does the applicant need to work in the elevator industry? Yes. The application requirements include information establishing that the applicant is primarily engaged in, or regularly employed by and intended to serve as the listed qualified individual for, a firm primarily engaged in a lawful elevator business. The NEC is the primary approved reference available during the SP-EL examination. Efficient navigation helps candidates locate motor, conductor, elevator, grounding, overcurrent, and wiring requirements without spending unnecessary testing time. Does passing the SP-EL examination automatically activate a contractor license? No. Passing the examination is part of the process. The applicable North Carolina electrical contractor license application and activation requirements must also be completed.

title: North Carolina NASCLA Master Electrical Contractor - Online Exam Prep
description: North Carolina NASCLA Master Electrical Contractor - Online Exam Prep Prepare for the North Carolina NASCLA Master Electrical Contractor licensing pathway with online exam prep focused on the NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors, also identified as the Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination. This preparation program is designed to strengthen National Electrical Code knowledge, electrical theory, calculations, project design, safety, wiring methods, equipment requirements, special occupancies, energy-efficiency concepts, and open-book reference navigation. The North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program and accepts the Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination. A candidate who has passed this NASCLA examination may use the examination result when applying for North Carolina electrical contracting classifications, subject to the experience, application, financial, qualifying-individual, and other requirements of the classification being requested. North Carolina electrical contractor licenses are issued in Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, and Special Restricted classifications. The NASCLA Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination is accepted for North Carolina licensing, but passing the examination by itself does not create a North Carolina license or eliminate the other qualifications established by the Board. The NASCLA examination is broader than a National Electrical Code-only test. Preparation includes electrical theory and principles, OSHA and NFPA 70E safety, project design and management, general code requirements, wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, electrical equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, and communication systems. The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors contains 100 scored questions. Candidates receive 270 minutes, or 4 hours and 30 minutes, to complete the examination and must answer at least 75 questions correctly to achieve the required 75% passing score. The examination is open book. Candidates should become familiar with the organization and navigation of every permitted reference before test day. The examination covers a large amount of electrical and construction material, so knowing which reference contains a particular type of information can be just as important as understanding the technical concept itself. The references associated with this preparation include the National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023, Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA), Delmar's Standard Textbook of Electricity, 6th Edition, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge, ANSI/ASHRAE/IES 90.1-2022, NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Basic 14th Edition, NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024, Ugly's Electrical References, and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications. What You Get Online NASCLA Electrical Exam Prep: Structured preparation for the NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors. 2023 NEC Review: Preparation involving the major National Electrical Code areas represented on the examination. Electrical Theory Practice: Review involving circuits, Ohm's Law, power, voltage, current, resistance, transformers, motors, and practical electrical calculations. Wiring and Protection Review: Preparation involving branch circuits, feeders, services, overcurrent protection, conductors, grounding, and bonding. Wiring Methods and Materials: Study involving raceways, cables, conductors, boxes, fittings, supports, conduit fill, and installation requirements. Project Design and Management: Preparation involving plans, specifications, estimating concepts, scheduling, coordination, risk, and project-management principles. Electrical Safety Review: Study involving OSHA construction safety and NFPA 70E workplace electrical safety. Reference Navigation: Practice identifying and locating information efficiently in the NEC, safety standards, electrical textbooks, project-management resources, and energy standards. Open-Book Exam Preparation: Study structure designed to improve technical understanding, calculations, and book-navigation efficiency under timed examination conditions. Exam Details The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is designed for Electrical Contractors, Master Electricians, and Unlimited Electricians. The examination contains 100 scored questions, allows 270 minutes, and requires a passing score of 75%. The examination content outline includes: Project Design and Management: 8 questions Safety: 9 questions Electrical Theory and Principles: 11 questions General Code Requirements: 17 questions Wiring and Protection: 17 questions Wiring Methods and Materials: 16 questions Equipment for General Use: 13 questions Special Occupancies, Special Equipment, and Special Conditions: 8 questions Communication Systems: 1 question General Code Requirements and Wiring and Protection are the largest individual categories with 17 questions each. Wiring Methods and Materials follows closely with 16 questions, while Equipment for General Use contributes 13 questions. Electrical Theory and Principles accounts for 11 questions. Safety contributes 9 questions. Project Design and Management and Special Occupancies, Special Equipment, and Special Conditions each contribute 8 questions. Together, General Code Requirements, Wiring and Protection, and Wiring Methods and Materials represent 50 of the 100 scored questions. Candidates should therefore become especially comfortable navigating and applying the 2023 National Electrical Code. Open Book Test The NASCLA Accredited Electrical Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates bring their permitted references to the examination center. References may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Permanent tabs may be used. Temporary tabs such as Post-it notes are not permitted, and references may not contain additional loose or attached papers. Open-book testing does not remove the need to learn the material. Candidates have approximately 2 minutes and 42 seconds per scored question, which means inefficient searching can consume a significant portion of the testing period. A productive study process combines technical review with reference navigation. Candidates should learn which books are most useful for different subjects before they begin timed practice. For example, a question involving conductor ampacity, grounding, branch circuits, raceways, services, feeders, motors, or special occupancies may require the 2023 NEC. A construction-jobsite safety question may lead to OSHA, while energized electrical work and arc-flash safety may require NFPA 70E. Electrical theory and calculation questions may be supported by Delmar's Standard Textbook of Electricity, Ugly's Electrical References, and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications. Project-management questions may require a different reference altogether. Licensing Steps Determine the North Carolina electrical classification you want. North Carolina issues Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, and several Special Restricted electrical contracting classifications. Confirm that you meet the applicable experience requirement. Experience requirements vary according to the North Carolina license classification being requested. Pass the NASCLA Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination. North Carolina accepts this NASCLA examination for applicable electrical contracting licensure. Send your NASCLA examination transcript to North Carolina. NASCLA examination results must be transmitted to the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors through the NASCLA National Examination Database process. Complete the North Carolina license application. Submit the application for the electrical contracting classification requested. Identify the qualified individual. North Carolina electrical contracting licenses require at least one listed qualified individual who is responsible for supervising and directing the electrical work performed under the license. Submit experience documentation. Provide the documentation required for the classification being requested. Complete financial requirements when applicable. Intermediate and Unlimited license applications are subject to additional financial-capacity requirements established by the Board. Complete final Board review. Passing NASCLA satisfies an accepted examination pathway, but the North Carolina license is issued only after the Board approves all applicable licensing requirements. State Requirements Electrical contracting in North Carolina is regulated by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. North Carolina law defines electrical contracting as engaging or offering to engage in the business of installing, maintaining, altering, or repairing electrical work, wiring, devices, appliances, or equipment. A business performing electrical contracting must hold the applicable license classification. North Carolina issues three principal electrical contracting classifications: Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited. It also offers several Special Restricted classifications for more limited types of electrical work. The Limited classification requires at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 2,000 hours of primary experience involving direct installation of electrical wiring and equipment governed by the National Electrical Code. The Intermediate classification requires at least 5,750 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 5,000 hours of primary electrical experience. The Unlimited classification requires at least 9,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 8,000 hours of primary experience. Unlimited applicants must also provide statements from individuals knowledgeable about the applicant's electrical experience and ability to supervise and direct electrical installation work. The Unlimited classification permits the licensee to engage in electrical contracting projects without a project-value limit. Limited and Intermediate licenses are subject to the project-value limits established for those classifications. The North Carolina Board accepts a passing NASCLA Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination for applicants seeking North Carolina electrical contracting licensure. Applicants who pass this NASCLA examination may apply for Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, or applicable Special Restricted classifications, subject to the requirements of the classification selected. North Carolina requires NASCLA-qualified applicants to have their examination transcripts sent to the Board through the NASCLA National Examination Database. Passing NASCLA does not create a national license and does not automatically produce a North Carolina electrical contractor license. The applicant must still complete the North Carolina licensing application and satisfy the applicable experience, financial, qualified-individual, and other Board requirements. Reference Books National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023Supports preparation involving general electrical requirements, branch circuits, feeders, services, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, conductors, raceways, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, and communication systems. Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)Supports preparation involving construction safety, electrical hazards, temporary power, personal protective equipment, ladders, scaffolds, tools, excavation, and other jobsite requirements. Delmar's Standard Textbook of Electricity, 6th EditionSupports preparation involving electrical theory, circuits, Ohm's Law, power, alternating current, transformers, motors, voltage, current, resistance, and practical calculations. A Guide to the Project Management Body of KnowledgeSupports preparation involving project planning, schedules, resources, risk, communication, coordination, quality, and project-management processes. ANSI/ASHRAE/IES 90.1-2022, Energy Standard for Sites and Buildings Except Low-Rise Residential Buildings - I-P EditionSupports preparation involving energy-efficiency requirements affecting commercial electrical systems, lighting, controls, and building energy performance. NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Basic 14th EditionSupports preparation involving project management, business organization, contracts, estimating, financial practices, risk management, safety, and construction-business principles. NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024Supports preparation involving shock hazards, arc-flash hazards, energized work, risk assessment, approach boundaries, personal protective equipment, and safe electrical work practices. Ugly's Electrical ReferencesSupports review of commonly used electrical formulas, tables, conductor information, motors, transformers, calculations, and practical field-reference information. Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC ApplicationsSupports preparation involving electrical theory and the practical application of electrical calculations and principles to National Electrical Code requirements. Test Information and Study Materials A strong preparation plan should begin with General Code Requirements, Wiring and Protection, and Wiring Methods and Materials. Together, these subjects account for half of the scored examination. Use the 2023 National Electrical Code regularly throughout preparation. Learn how Chapters 1 through 9 are organized and become comfortable moving between broad requirements and articles covering specific equipment or installation conditions. General Code Requirements preparation should include terminology, equipment installation, working space, identification, approvals, listing and labeling concepts, and general NEC provisions that affect multiple types of electrical installations. Wiring and Protection preparation should include branch circuits, feeders, services, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, conductor ampacity, loads, and protection of electrical systems. Wiring Methods and Materials should include raceways, cables, conductors, boxes, fittings, supports, conduit fill, box fill, installation conditions, and protection from physical damage. Equipment for General Use accounts for 13 questions. Review motors, transformers, appliances, generators, luminaires, equipment connections, and other commonly encountered electrical equipment. Electrical Theory and Principles accounts for 11 questions. Practice Ohm's Law, power formulas, series and parallel circuits, voltage, current, resistance, impedance, alternating current, transformer relationships, and other trade calculations. Use Delmar's Standard Textbook of Electricity, Ugly's Electrical References, and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications to reinforce calculations and electrical fundamentals. Safety represents 9 questions. Review OSHA and NFPA 70E as separate but related safety resources. OSHA addresses broad construction-jobsite requirements, while NFPA 70E focuses on electrical workplace hazards and safe electrical work practices. Study shock hazards, arc-flash hazards, electrical protective equipment, energized work concepts, personal protective equipment, temporary electrical systems, ladders, tools, and other jobsite hazards. Project Design and Management accounts for 8 questions. Review project planning, documentation, scheduling, resources, coordination, communication, quality, estimating concepts, and risk management. Special Occupancies, Special Equipment, and Special Conditions also accounts for 8 questions. Become familiar with the NEC chapters that address installations requiring additional or modified electrical rules. Many NEC questions require candidates to connect general code provisions with a more specific article. Practice following references rather than stopping after locating the first section that appears relevant. ANSI/ASHRAE/IES 90.1-2022 should be reviewed for commercial energy requirements affecting electrical and lighting systems. Learn the organization of the standard so applicable provisions can be located efficiently. Reference navigation should be integrated into practice from the beginning. Read the question, identify the principal subject, choose the likely reference, and then begin the lookup. A question about arc flash should suggest NFPA 70E rather than a random NEC search. A construction fall-protection question should suggest OSHA. A calculation involving electrical theory may be faster to solve with the theory references than by searching code articles. For NEC questions, learn to use the index strategically. Identify the primary electrical term, find the term in the index, move to the cited article or section, and then verify whether additional provisions apply. Practice common calculations until you can recognize which formula is required before consulting a reference. This can save time on questions involving current, voltage, resistance, power, motors, transformers, and conductor calculations. With 100 scored questions in 270 minutes, time management matters. Candidates should answer familiar questions efficiently and avoid allowing one difficult lookup to consume excessive testing time. As examination day approaches, transition from isolated subject review into mixed-topic practice. Move between NEC code questions, electrical theory, OSHA, NFPA 70E, equipment, special occupancies, project management, and energy requirements. For North Carolina licensing preparation, candidates should separately become familiar with the classification they intend to request. A passing NASCLA result can support applications for different North Carolina electrical contracting classifications, but each classification retains its own experience and licensing requirements. How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal 1 Exam Prep supports North Carolina NASCLA Master Electrical Contractor candidates through organized study guidance, electrical trade review, calculation practice, code navigation, project-management preparation, and confidence-building study structure. Candidates can practice deciding which reference is appropriate and locating the supporting technical information efficiently. Practice-oriented preparation helps reinforce code relationships, calculations, terminology, electrical theory, safety concepts, and equipment requirements instead of depending only on passive reading. The goal is to help candidates approach the NASCLA Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination with stronger electrical knowledge, better NEC-navigation skills, improved calculation confidence, greater safety awareness, and an organized study process without guaranteeing a passing score or North Carolina license. The NASCLA Accredited Electrical Contractor examination is an open-book test. Does North Carolina accept the NASCLA Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician exam? Yes. A candidate who has passed the NASCLA Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination may apply for North Carolina electrical contracting classifications, including Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, and applicable Special Restricted classifications, subject to the requirements for the classification selected. Does passing NASCLA automatically give me a North Carolina Unlimited electrical license? No. Applicants seeking Unlimited licensure must also satisfy North Carolina's experience, application, qualified-individual, financial, and other applicable requirements. How much experience is required for a North Carolina Unlimited electrical contractor applicant? The Unlimited classification requires at least 9,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 8,000 hours of primary electrical experience. How much experience is required for the North Carolina Intermediate classification? The Intermediate classification requires at least 5,750 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 5,000 hours of primary electrical experience. How much experience is required for the North Carolina Limited classification? The Limited classification requires at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 2,000 hours of primary electrical experience. Does the NASCLA exam use the 2023 National Electrical Code? Yes. The 2023 National Electrical Code is included among the references used for this preparation. What are the largest sections of the NASCLA Electrical Contractor exam? General Code Requirements and Wiring and Protection each contain 17 questions, followed by Wiring Methods and Materials with 16 questions. Does the exam cover electrical theory? Yes. Electrical Theory and Principles accounts for 11 questions. Does the exam include OSHA and NFPA 70E safety? Yes. NASCLA-qualified applicants must have their examination transcript sent to the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors through the NASCLA National Examination Database process. Does passing the NASCLA examination create a national electrical license? No. NASCLA provides an accredited trade examination accepted by participating licensing agencies. Candidates must apply separately and satisfy the licensing requirements of each jurisdiction. Does this online exam prep guarantee that I will pass? description: North Carolina NASCLA Residential Electrician Exam Book Package Prepare for the North Carolina NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination with a complete reference-book package covering residential electrical code, electrical theory, construction safety, workplace electrical safety, contractor business and project management, fire alarm systems, product safety information, and residential construction requirements. The North Carolina NASCLA Residential Electrician Exam Book Package brings together nine references that support organized preparation for the NASCLA Accredited Residential Electrical Contractor examination and North Carolina's Special Restricted Single-Family Residential Dwelling electrical contractor licensing pathway. The North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program. North Carolina accepts the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination in lieu of the North Carolina SP-SFD Single-Family Detached Residential Dwelling examination. Candidates who pass the accepted NASCLA examination may apply for the SP-SFD classification, but they must still satisfy North Carolina's licensing requirements. The SP-SFD classification is a special restricted electrical contracting license focused on electrical wiring and devices installed in or on single-family residential dwellings and qualifying ancillary structures. This makes the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination relevant to electrical professionals seeking a North Carolina residential-focused electrical contracting credential. This book package includes the National Electrical Code 2023, Code of Federal Regulations 29 CFR Part 1926, NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management 14th edition, NFPA 70E 2024, Ugly's Electrical References, NFPA 72 2022, Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications, ANSI Z535.4-2023, and the International Residential Code 2024. What You Get National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023 Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA) NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, 14th NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024 Ugly's Electrical References NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm Code, 2022 Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications ANSI Z535.4-2023, Product Safety Signs and Labels International Residential Code (IRC), 2024 Together, these references provide a broad study library for residential electrical code navigation, electrical calculations, construction safety, workplace electrical safety, fire alarm systems, residential building requirements, product safety communication, electrical theory, and contractor business knowledge. Candidates can use the books together to develop a practical study routine that connects code requirements with real-world residential electrical work. Exam Details The NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program offers standardized electrical trade examinations for participating licensing agencies. The program includes examinations for Electrical Contractors or Master Electricians, Journeyman Electricians, and Residential Electrical Contractors. North Carolina currently accepts the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination specifically for eligibility toward the Special Restricted Single-Family Residential Dwelling, or SP-SFD, license. The North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors instructs applicants using this pathway to have their NASCLA examination transcripts sent to the Board as part of the application process. The NASCLA examination is not a national license. Passing the examination satisfies an accepted trade-examination requirement for participating agencies, while each jurisdiction continues to enforce its own experience, application, licensing, and scope-of-work requirements. Residential electrical exam preparation should include subjects such as: Electrical theory and calculations General National Electrical Code requirements Residential services and service equipment Feeders and branch circuits Dwelling-unit electrical requirements Conductor sizing and ampacity Overcurrent protection Grounding and bonding Residential wiring methods and materials Raceways, cables, boxes, and enclosures Equipment and appliances Electrical safety Construction-site safety Fire alarm and signaling systems Residential construction requirements Electrical theory and practical problem solving Contractor business, law, and project management Strong preparation should combine technical study with regular reference navigation. Residential electrical questions often require candidates to connect several subjects, such as load calculations, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, and the applicable National Electrical Code requirements. Open Book Test The NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination is an open book test. NASCLA identifies its Residential Electrical Contractor examination as one of the open-book electrical trade examinations offered through the Accredited Electrical Examination Program. Open-book testing makes reference familiarity an important part of preparation. Candidates should develop a repeatable method for identifying the subject of a question, selecting the correct book, locating the applicable code provision, definition, table, formula, or safety rule, and then applying that information correctly. The National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023 should receive significant attention. Candidates should become comfortable with Article 100 definitions, the index, article organization, tables, exceptions, notes, and cross-references. Residential preparation should include services, feeders, branch circuits, receptacles, lighting outlets, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, equipment, appliances, and special systems. Electrical theory should be studied alongside code navigation. Review voltage, current, resistance, power, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, alternating-current principles, loads, motors, transformers, and practical calculations. Understanding the electrical principle behind a question can make it easier to determine which code provision or formula applies. OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 supports construction-safety preparation, while NFPA 70E addresses electrical workplace safety. NFPA 72 supports fire alarm and signaling-system study. The International Residential Code adds broader residential construction context that can help candidates understand the physical environments in which residential electrical systems are installed. Ugly's Electrical References and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications support formulas, calculations, and technical concepts. ANSI Z535.4-2023 addresses product safety signs and labels, while the NASCLA Contractors Guide supports contractor business and project-management study. Licensing Steps Passing the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination does not automatically issue a North Carolina electrical contractor license. Candidates must complete the licensing process through the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Identify the SP-SFD classification. North Carolina accepts the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination for the Special Restricted Single-Family Residential Dwelling license. Review the experience requirements. Applicants must satisfy the Board's qualifying experience requirements for the SP-SFD classification. Prepare the license application. Applicants must submit the required application and supporting documentation to the Board. Provide character documentation. Examination applicants must submit written statements from at least two people attesting to the applicant's good character. Complete the NASCLA examination process. Apply for and pass the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination. Send the NASCLA transcript to North Carolina. Applicants using the NASCLA pathway must have the examination transcript transmitted to the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Document qualifying electrical experience. Provide the experience information needed to establish eligibility for the SP-SFD classification. Complete the Board's licensing review. The Board determines whether the applicant satisfies all licensing requirements before issuing the SP-SFD credential. State Requirements Electrical contractor licensing in North Carolina is regulated by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. The Board issues several electrical contractor classifications, including Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, and special restricted classifications. For the SP-SFD Single-Family Detached Residential Dwelling classification, current Board rules require at least 3,000 hours of qualifying electrical experience. At least 2,000 hours must be primary experience, while the remaining qualifying hours may be primary experience, secondary experience, or a combination of both. North Carolina defines primary experience as work directly involving the installation of electrical wiring and equipment governed by the National Electrical Code or activities directly related to that work. Qualifying primary experience can include work as a journeyman electrician, electrical mechanic, electrical foreman, electrical superintendent, electrical estimator for a licensed contractor, and other qualifying electrical roles recognized by the Board. Applicants for an electrical contracting examination must also be at least 18 years of age, submit the required application, and provide written statements from at least two people attesting to good character. The SP-SFD classification authorizes the licensee to install, maintain, or repair electrical wiring and devices that are in or on a single-family residential dwelling or ancillary to that dwelling. For purposes of the SP-SFD classification, North Carolina defines a single-family residential dwelling as a building or manufactured home designed and used for habitation by one family and not physically attached to another building or structure. Qualifying cabanas, porches, room additions, and ancillary structures can be treated as part of the single-family dwelling when they are designed and used for residential purposes. Ancillary structures associated with the dwelling can include detached residential garages or carports, household or farm equipment storage buildings, barns, pump houses, electric fences, and yard lighting when the work falls within the authorized residential scope. The SP-SFD classification is more limited than North Carolina's broader Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited electrical contractor licenses. Candidates pursuing the residential classification should understand the specific scope of work authorized by the SP-SFD credential before contracting for electrical projects. North Carolina's acceptance of NASCLA does not remove these state requirements. The NASCLA examination serves as an accepted trade-examination pathway, while experience, character, application, licensing, and scope requirements remain under the authority of the North Carolina Board. Reference Books National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023The primary electrical code reference supporting preparation involving residential services, feeders, branch circuits, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, equipment, appliances, and special electrical systems. Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)A construction-industry safety reference covering occupational safety and health requirements relevant to construction jobsites, electrical work, equipment, tools, and workplace hazards. NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, 14thA contractor-focused reference supporting study of business organization, contracts, project management, estimating, financial management, employment responsibilities, safety management, and professional contractor operations. NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024An electrical workplace safety reference addressing safe-work practices and procedures intended to reduce exposure to electrical hazards. Ugly's Electrical ReferencesA compact electrical field reference containing commonly used formulas, tables, conversions, calculations, and practical electrical information for theory and problem-solving preparation. NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm Code, 2022A reference supporting preparation involving fire alarm and signaling systems, detection, initiating devices, notification functions, circuits, and related system requirements. Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC ApplicationsA study reference focused on voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, calculations, and the relationship between electrical theory and practical National Electrical Code applications. ANSI Z535.4-2023, Product Safety Signs and LabelsA safety standard addressing product safety signs and labels used to communicate hazards, warnings, cautions, and other important safety information. International Residential Code (IRC), 2024A residential construction reference supporting understanding of dwelling construction and the building conditions in which residential electrical systems are installed. Test Information and Study Materials A productive North Carolina NASCLA Residential Electrician study plan should combine electrical code review, electrical theory, calculations, construction safety, workplace electrical safety, residential construction knowledge, fire alarm systems, and contractor business topics. Begin with the 2023 National Electrical Code. Study residential services, feeders, branch circuits, load calculations, conductor ampacity, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, receptacle requirements, lighting outlets, boxes, raceways, cables, appliances, motors, and electrical equipment. Practice navigating the NEC rather than trying to memorize every provision. Learn how to use the index, Article 100 definitions, individual articles, tables, exceptions, and cross-references. Open-book preparation is more effective when candidates know how to locate information from several starting points. Review electrical theory throughout preparation. Practice Ohm's law, voltage, current, resistance, power, series and parallel circuits, alternating-current fundamentals, loads, motors, and transformers. Ugly's Electrical References and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications can reinforce these concepts. Use OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 for construction safety and NFPA 70E for electrical workplace safety. NFPA 72 supports preparation involving fire alarm and signaling systems. ANSI Z535.4-2023 adds product safety communication concepts, while the International Residential Code provides broader residential construction context. Use the NASCLA Contractors Guide to review contractor-focused subjects such as business operations, contracts, estimating, project management, financial concepts, employment responsibilities, and safety management. Practice-oriented study should include active use of the books. Identify the subject of a question, choose the appropriate reference, locate the applicable code section, safety provision, formula, or technical requirement, and then apply it to the problem. How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal 1 Exam Prep supports residential electrical candidates through organized study guidance, trade-focused review, practice-oriented preparation, reference navigation, and confidence-building study structure. The North Carolina NASCLA Residential Electrician Exam Book Package provides a strong reference foundation for candidates preparing for the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination. Trade-focused study helps connect related subjects rather than treating individual code provisions as isolated facts. A residential service problem may require load calculations, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, electrical theory, and multiple National Electrical Code provisions. Practice-oriented preparation encourages candidates to actively use their references. Working through questions, identifying the correct book, locating the supporting information, and applying the requirement or formula helps reinforce technical knowledge and reference familiarity. Reference-navigation practice is especially useful for an open-book examination. Regular use of the NEC, OSHA regulations, NFPA standards, residential code, theory materials, and contractor guide can help candidates become more comfortable finding information efficiently. The study process can also help identify areas that need additional attention. Candidates may choose to spend more time on services, feeders, load calculations, grounding and bonding, conductor sizing, wiring methods, electrical theory, fire alarm systems, workplace safety, or contractor business subjects based on their individual study needs. 1 Exam Prep is designed to help candidates strengthen residential electrical knowledge, improve familiarity with the reference library, and build an organized exam-preparation routine without guaranteeing a particular test result or licensing outcome. North Carolina accepts the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination for applicants pursuing the Special Restricted Single-Family Residential Dwelling, or SP-SFD, electrical contractor license. Is the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination open book? Yes. NASCLA identifies the Residential Electrical Contractor examination as an open-book electrical trade examination using authorized references under the applicable testing rules. Which North Carolina license corresponds to the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor exam? The accepted NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination can be used toward the SP-SFD Special Restricted Single-Family Residential Dwelling license. How much experience is required for North Carolina SP-SFD? Current North Carolina Board rules require at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 2,000 hours of primary electrical experience. What work can an SP-SFD license holder perform? The classification authorizes qualifying electrical installation, maintenance, and repair work in or on single-family residential dwellings and qualifying ancillary structures associated with those dwellings. Do I need to send my NASCLA transcript to North Carolina? Yes. North Carolina requires applicants using the NASCLA pathway to have the applicable NASCLA examination transcript sent to the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Does passing NASCLA automatically issue a North Carolina license? No. Passing the accepted NASCLA examination satisfies an examination component. Applicants must still satisfy North Carolina's experience, character, application, and licensing requirements. Which books are included in this package? The package includes the NEC 2023, OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926, NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management 14th edition, NFPA 70E 2024, Ugly's Electrical References, NFPA 72 2022, Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications, ANSI Z535.4-2023, and IRC 2024. Why is the NEC important for residential electrical exam preparation? The NEC contains essential requirements involving services, feeders, branch circuits, conductors, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, equipment, and other electrical installations. Strong NEC navigation is an important part of open-book preparation. Why is the International Residential Code included? The IRC provides broader residential construction context and helps candidates understand the building environments in which residential electrical wiring, equipment, and systems are installed. How should I use the book package to prepare? Study by subject and actively use the references while working practice-oriented questions. Identify the topic, choose the appropriate book, locate the supporting provision or formula, and apply the information. Repeated navigation can strengthen both technical knowledge and familiarity with the reference library.

Exam Details The North Carolina Residential Contractor Examination is administered by PSI Examination Services for the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors (NCLBGC). This examination evaluates knowledge associated with residential construction methods, building systems, construction safety, estimating, code requirements, and contractor responsibilities. Exam Name: North Carolina Residential Contractor Examination State: North Carolina Licensing Authority: North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors Testing Provider: PSI Examination Services Number of Questions: 90 Time Allowed: 210 minutes (3 hours and 30 minutes) Passing Score: 70% Exam Format: Open-book examination Exam Classification: Residential Contractor The examination includes a variety of subjects relevant to residential building construction. Candidates are expected to understand technical concepts, recognize construction terminology, interpret plans and specifications, and demonstrate familiarity with applicable building regulations. The official examination content outline identifies the following subject areas: Site Work, Footings, and Foundations – 12 questions Concrete and Concrete Reinforcement – 10 questions Masonry – 7 questions Carpentry – 11 questions Associated Construction Trades, Including Energy Conservation and Drywall – 8 questions Roofing – 6 questions Estimating, Plan Reading, and General Residential Code Requirements – 16 questions OSHA Safety – 4 questions Licensing, Business, and Law – 10 questions Special Construction Zones, Including Wind and Coastal Requirements, and Erosion and Sedimentation Control – 6 questions Because the examination covers a broad range of topics, effective preparation involves more than concentrating on one construction specialty. Open Book Test The North Carolina Residential Contractor Exam is an open-book examination. Candidates are permitted to bring specific approved reference materials into the testing center in accordance with PSI examination rules. Although the exam is open book, preparation remains essential. Candidates must understand the construction concepts presented in examination questions and be able to locate relevant information efficiently within approved reference materials. With 90 questions and 210 minutes available, time management plays an important role. Spending excessive time searching for individual answers can reduce the time available for completing other questions. North Carolina Residential Contractor Exam Study Flash Cards can help reinforce construction terminology and technical concepts through repeated review. Licensing Steps Obtaining a North Carolina Residential Contractor license involves meeting the requirements established by the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. The licensing process includes application review, qualification requirements, and examination requirements associated with the residential classification. Review the Residential Contractor Classification: Understand the scope of residential construction activities covered by the North Carolina Residential Contractor license. Determine the Appropriate License Limitation: Review the available license limitations and the financial qualifications associated with the level of contracting work you intend to perform. Review Applicant Qualifications: Become familiar with the Board's eligibility, financial responsibility, and application requirements. Submit the Licensing Application: Complete the required application process with the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors. Prepare for the Residential Contractor Examination: Develop a study schedule using construction references, examination preparation resources, and study flash cards. Schedule and Complete the Examination: Follow the examination authorization and scheduling procedures provided by the Board and PSI. Complete Remaining Licensing Requirements: Satisfy applicable Board requirements for the requested classification and license limitation. North Carolina uses a qualifying individual system in which an individual who has passed the applicable examination can serve as a qualifier for the license applicant. The qualifying individual and the licensed contractor may be separate legal persons or entities. Preparing for the examination is therefore an important step toward meeting the technical qualification component of the licensing process. State Requirements The North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors regulates general contractor licensing under North Carolina law. Individuals and businesses seeking to perform work covered by the state's general contractor licensing requirements must meet the applicable licensing standards. North Carolina generally requires a general contractor license for construction projects with a total cost of $40,000 or more, subject to applicable statutory provisions and exemptions. The Residential Contractor classification covers construction and demolition activities involving residential units required to comply with the residential building code adopted by the North Carolina Building Code Council. The classification also encompasses related site work, driveways, sidewalks, and ancillary water and wastewater systems, along with certain specialty construction activities performed as part of residential construction. Applicants must satisfy the Board's eligibility requirements, which include minimum age, good moral character, financial responsibility, and applicable application and background-check requirements. North Carolina also establishes different general contractor license limitations. These limitations determine the maximum value of projects a licensed contractor may undertake and are connected to financial qualification requirements. Residential Contractor examination candidates benefit from understanding both construction knowledge and the regulatory responsibilities associated with working as a licensed contractor. Test Information and Study Materials The North Carolina Residential Contractor Exam covers construction topics that require both practical understanding and familiarity with technical standards. Site Work, Footings, and Foundations: Review site preparation, soil considerations, excavation, foundation terminology, drainage principles, and the relationship between foundations and residential structural systems. Residential Building Code Requirements: Become familiar with the organization and application of the residential code, including structural, safety, and construction provisions relevant to residential buildings. OSHA Safety: Review construction workplace safety principles, hazard recognition, and practices intended to reduce risks during construction operations. Licensing, Business, and Law: Strengthen understanding of contractor licensing responsibilities, construction business concepts, project administration, and general legal terminology. Wind, Coastal, and Erosion Requirements: Develop familiarity with special construction considerations involving environmental conditions, wind exposure, coastal construction, and erosion and sedimentation control.
